順天府鄉試錄序

聖天子握符御宇，覃敷文治，薄海內外沐德嚮風。章甫縫掖之流，砥志勵業，竢應賢科。有司祗若成典，益飭以虔。嘉靖壬子秋八月，維鄉試之期，順天府府丞臣鏜職在提調，以例請。上命左庶子臣朴、修撰臣鳴雷往典考試。同考試教授臣國政，教諭臣思、臣澤、臣希古、臣澤、臣順吉、臣一元、臣功甫、臣成春，監試御史臣逢時、臣瑞登，
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

The sagely Son of Heaven holds the mandate and rules the realm, extending civil governance far and wide. Throughout the lands within and beyond the seas, all bathe in his virtue and turn toward his transforming influence. Scholars wearing the ritual cap and broad-sleeved robes steel their resolve and diligently pursue their studies, awaiting the examination that selects the worthy. The responsible officials reverently follow established statutes, attending to their duties with still greater care and devotion. In the eighth month of autumn in the renzi year of Jiajing [1552], when the Provincial Examination was due, your servant Tang 鏜, Vice Prefect of Shuntian Prefecture, whose duty was to serve as Proctor, submitted a request in accordance with precedent. His Majesty ordered your servants Pu 朴, Left Secretariat Supervisor of the Heir Apparent, and Minglei 鳴雷, Senior Compiler, to go and preside as Examiners. Serving as Associate Examiners were your servant Guozheng 國政, Prefectural School Instructor, and your servants Si 思, Ze 澤, Xigu 希古, Ze 澤, Shunji 順吉, Yiyuan 一元, Gongfu 功甫, and Chengchun 成春, County School Instructors; the censors supervising the examination were your servants Fengshi 逢時 and Ruideng 瑞登…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
其諸執事咸遴以充七日丁
巳入簾臣朴一芥草茅幸際
聖明再役校文誓精白一心仰荅
鴻恩乃合六館諸曹暨提學御
史臣阮鶚所選士三試之遵
制額校取百三十五人成錄以
獻臣朴謹爲序曰昔孔子論周
===
道之美褒贊當代之人才曰
唐虞之際於斯爲盛謂初盛
於唐虞再盛於周也臣讀大
雅諸篇觀周人才之盛盖有
四徵焉夫文王至德造周化
洽豐芑山川效靈寔生衆哲
其詩曰思皇多士生此王國

===
道之美褒賛當代之人才曰
唐虞之際於斯爲盛謂初盛
於唐虞再盛於周也〔臣〕讀大
雅諸篇觀周人才之盛盖有
四徵焉夫文王至德造周化
洽豐芑山川效靈寔生衆哲
其詩曰思皇多士生此王國
punctuated:
其諸執事，咸遴以充。七日丁巳，入簾。臣朴一芥草茅，幸際聖明，再役校文，誓精白一心，仰荅鴻恩。乃合六館諸曹暨提學御史臣阮鶚所選士，三試之，遵制額校取百三十五人，成錄以獻。臣朴謹爲序曰：
昔孔子論周道之美，褒贊當代之人才曰：「唐虞之際，於斯爲盛。」謂初盛於唐虞，再盛於周也。臣讀《大雅》諸篇，觀周人才之盛，盖有四徵焉。夫文王至德造周，化洽豐芑，山川效靈，寔生衆哲。其詩曰：「思皇多士，生此王國
translation_en:
…All the other functionaries were carefully selected to fill their posts. On the seventh day, dingsi, we entered the examination enclosure. Your servant Pu, an insignificant man of humble origins, has had the good fortune to live under a sage and enlightened ruler and to be assigned a second time to evaluate examination essays. I vowed to devote myself with a pure and single heart to repaying the vast imperial favor. We therefore assembled the candidates from the six colleges and the various offices, together with those selected by your servant Ruan E, the Education Censor, and examined them in three sessions. In accordance with the prescribed quota, we evaluated and selected 135 men, and compiled this record for presentation to the throne. Your servant Pu respectfully submits the following preface:
In former times, Confucius, discussing the excellence of the Way of Zhou, praised the talented men of that age, saying: “From the time of Tang and Yu, talent was most abundant in this age.” This means that talent first flourished under Tang and Yu, and flourished again under Zhou. Reading the poems of the Greater Odes, your servant has observed four indications of the abundance of talent under Zhou. King Wen established Zhou through his consummate virtue; his transforming influence pervaded Feng and Qi [?], and the mountains and rivers manifested their numinous power, bringing forth many wise men. The poem says: “Splendid were the many worthy men, born in this royal kingdom…”

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
王國克生維周之楨言生賢
有自也可以徵地焉聖人乆
道化成人文丕變其詩曰周
王壽考遐不作人言成賢有
本也可以徵化焉賢不虛生
乘時嚮用期顯厥蘊其詩曰
鳳凰鳴矣于彼高岡梧桐生
===
矣于彼朝陽言賢志於用也
可以徵幾焉股肱經綸咸效
厥能升于大猷其詩曰予曰
有疏附予曰有先後予曰有
奔奏予曰有禦侮言賢益于
國也可以徵忠焉譬諸嘉穀
地言乎其植也化言乎其培

punctuated: 王國克生，維周之楨。」言生賢有自也，可以徵地焉。聖人乆道化成，人文丕變。其詩曰：「周王壽考，遐不作人。」言成賢有本也，可以徵化焉。賢不虛生，乘時嚮用，期顯厥蘊。其詩曰：「鳳凰鳴矣，于彼高岡；梧桐生矣，于彼朝陽。」言賢志於用也，可以徵幾焉。股肱經綸，咸效厥能，升于大猷。其詩曰：「予曰有疏附，予曰有先後，予曰有奔奏，予曰有禦侮。」言賢益于國也，可以徵忠焉。譬諸嘉穀，地言乎其植也，化言乎其培
translation_en: …“The royal domain can indeed bring them forth: they are the pillars of Zhou.” This says that the birth of worthy men has a source; here one may find evidence of the influence of place. The sage perseveres in the Way and brings his transforming influence to fruition, profoundly changing human culture. The poem says: “May the king of Zhou enjoy long life! Does he not nurture men?” This says that the formation of worthy men has a foundation; here one may find evidence of transforming influence. Worthy men are not born in vain: they seize their moment and aspire to employment, hoping to reveal the abilities they possess. The poem says: “The phoenix cries upon that high ridge; the parasol tree grows upon its sunlit eastern slope.” This says that worthy men aspire to serve; here one may find evidence of timely opportunity. As the ruler’s limbs, they put affairs in order, all giving full scope to their abilities and advancing the great plan of government. The poem says: “I say there are those who draw others close; I say there are those who guide and assist; I say there are those who hasten in service; I say there are those who repel aggression.” This says that worthy men benefit the state; here one may find evidence of loyalty. To compare them to fine grain: place refers to its planting, transforming influence to its cultivation…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
也幾言乎其茂也忠言乎其
實也孔子才難之歎郁郁之
稱有以哉夫燕薊幽趙今之
王國也我
太祖拓靖中夏以北方人文未著
命師頒籍恒注意焉
成祖奠鼎燕都環列畿輔密邇
===

列聖紹統滋培孔厚矧其形勝實

皇上斂福錫民三紀于茲光被風
動徧於六合作人之效邁周
遠矣遐壤僻隅咸獲登遂矧

translation_en: …; discernment of incipient signs refers to its luxuriant growth, and loyalty to its fruit. Confucius had good reason to lament how hard talent is to find and to praise the flourishing culture of Zhou! The lands of Yan, Ji, You, and Zhao now constitute the royal domain. Our Taizu expanded and pacified the central realm. Because cultural accomplishment in the north was not yet conspicuous, he appointed teachers and distributed books, keeping this constantly in mind. Chengzu established his capital at Yanjing. The surrounding metropolitan territories, close to the imperial transforming influence, took precedence in attendance at court and submission. Successive sage emperors continued the imperial line, nurturing these lands most generously. Moreover, their strategic configuration truly makes them a naturally endowed stronghold, where two can withstand a hundred. They should surely produce outstanding men and talents renowned in their age, pillars sustaining the state. Our present emperor has gathered blessings and bestowed them upon the people for three twelve-year cycles now. His radiance reaches everywhere, and his influence moves all throughout the six directions. His achievements in cultivating men of talent far surpass those of Zhou! Even distant lands and remote corners have all gained opportunities for advancement and fulfillment; how much more…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
首善地乎宜其德造譽髦丕昭
聖皇之化也夫士生
王國被
皇化際
聖主誠希曠之遇千載之幾也孰
無功業願哉顧其始在定其
志耳盖士必有弘毅正直之
===
志而後有光明俊偉之業否
或汨於俗移於利鶩於名則
才之適用者浮而功之益于
國者微忠何有焉夫始也志不
預定而終也至不能成其忠
可懼也已茲諸士以經術錄
于有司寔嚮用之始盍定厥

punctuated:
首善地乎？宜其德造譽髦，丕昭聖皇之化也。
夫士生王國，被皇化，際聖主，誠希曠之遇、千載之幾也。孰無功業願哉？顧其始在定其志耳。盖士必有弘毅正直之志，而後有光明俊偉之業。否，或汨於俗，移於利，鶩於名，則才之適用者浮，而功之益于國者微，忠何有焉？夫始也志不預定，而終也至不能成其忠，可懼也已！
茲諸士以經術錄于有司，寔嚮用之始，盍定厥
translation_en:
…the foremost seat of goodness? It is fitting that its men should be cultivated in virtue and renowned for excellence, splendidly manifesting the sage emperor’s transforming influence.
For a scholar to be born in the royal realm, receive the emperor’s transforming influence, and encounter a sage ruler is truly an exceedingly rare good fortune, an opportunity that comes once in a thousand years. Who would not aspire to achievement? Yet the first step lies simply in firmly setting one’s purpose. Only when a scholar possesses a purpose that is broad-minded, resolute, upright, and honest can he accomplish deeds that are illustrious and outstanding. Otherwise, if he becomes submerged in prevailing customs, swayed by profit, or intent upon fame, his talents will prove superficial in practical application, and his accomplishments will bring little benefit to the state. Where, then, is his loyalty? If he fails to establish his purpose at the outset and ultimately proves unable to fulfill his loyalty, that is indeed cause for fear!

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
志以成厥忠乎是故體
國庇民端其衷陳力宣猷達其
義貞誠弼亮弘其業周計預
慮永其休以匹美於思皇周
楨之士斯嘉穀之實也其於
際遘之茂
化育之培
===
王國之產無媿負矣校文者尚
亦有榮問哉詩曰藹藹王多
吉士維君子使媚于天子我
皇上化成之效也又曰庶幾夙夜
以永終譽敢用是爲諸士規
奉議大夫左春坊左庶子兼
翰林院侍讀郭朴謹序

義貞誠弼亮弘其業周計預
慮永其休以匹美於思皇周
楨之士斯嘉穀之實也其於
際遘之茂
化育之培
===
王國之產無忝負矣校文者尚
亦有榮閒哉詩曰藹藹王多
吉士維君子使媚于天子我
皇上化成之效也又曰庶幾夙夜
以永終譽敢用是爲諸士規
奉議大夫左春坊左庶子兼
翰林院侍讀郭〔朴〕謹序
punctuated:
志，以成厥忠乎？是故體國庇民，端其衷；陳力宣猷，達其義；貞誠弼亮，弘其業；周計預慮，永其休，以匹美於思皇周楨之士，斯嘉穀之實也。其於際遘之茂、化育之培、王國之產，無媿負矣。校文者尚亦有榮問哉！詩曰：「藹藹王多吉士，維君子使，媚于天子。」我皇上化成之效也。又曰：「庶幾夙夜，以永終譽。」敢用是爲諸士規。
奉議大夫、左春坊左庶子兼翰林院侍讀郭朴謹序。
translation_en:
…resolve, so as to fulfill their loyalty? Thus, by caring for the state and sheltering the people, they rectify their hearts; by exerting their strength and advancing sound counsels, they put righteousness into practice; by steadfast sincerity and loyal assistance, they enlarge their achievements; and by comprehensive planning and foresight, they make their beneficent work endure. In this way they may rival those admirable men who were the pillars of Zhou: these are indeed the ripened fruits of fine grain. They will then have proved worthy of their splendid opportunities, the nurturing influence that cultivated them, and the royal realm that produced them. Might those who evaluated their writings also gain an honored reputation thereby?
The Book of Odes says: “In multitudes, the king has many worthy men; these gentlemen are employed, and are cherished by the Son of Heaven.” This is the effect of our Emperor’s transforming and perfecting influence. It also says: “May you strive morning and night, to preserve your good name to the end.” I venture to offer these words as an admonition to you gentlemen.
Preface respectfully composed by Guo Pu 郭朴, Grand Master for Consultative Service, Left Junior Supervisor of Instruction in the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently Reader-in-Waiting in the Hanlin Academy.

Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination, thirty-first year of Jiajing (1552)

Proctor
Ye Tang, Vice Prefect of Shuntian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Rusheng; he was from Shangrao County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the xinchou year.

Examiners
Guo Pu, Grand Master for Counsel, Left Vice Supervisor of the Household in the Left Spring Office, concurrently Reader-in-waiting in the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Zhifu; he was from Anyang County, Henan, and was a metropolitan graduate of the yiwei year.
Qin Minglei, Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman for Erudition. His courtesy name was Ziyu; he was from Linhai County, Zhejiang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the jiachen year.

Associate Examiners
Zhang Guozheng, Professor in the Confucian School of Taiyuan Prefecture, Shanxi. His courtesy name was Yunzhi; he was from Wei County, Shandong, and was a tribute student (gongshi) of the renwu year.
Hu En, Instructor in the Confucian School of Changshu County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region (Zhili). His courtesy name was Tingxi; he was from Luling County, Jiangxi, and was a tribute student of the guimao year.
Jiang Ze, Instructor in the Confucian School of Shucheng County, Luzhou Prefecture, Zhili. His courtesy name was Ziren; he was from Macheng County, Huguang, and was a tribute student of the jiyou year.
Wei Xigu, Instructor in the Confucian School of Ganyu County, Haizhou Subprefecture, Huai'an Prefecture, Zhili. His courtesy name was Ruxue; he was from the Guilin Central Guard, Guangxi, and was a tribute student of the guimao year.
Hu Ze, Instructor in the Confucian School of Huoshan County, Lu'an Subprefecture, Luzhou Prefecture, Zhili. His courtesy name was Zishu; he was from Tongcheng County, Huguang, and was a tribute student of the jiyou year.
Zhao Shunji, Instructor in the Confucian School of Chongde County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang. His courtesy name was Zhengfu; he was from Neijiang County, Sichuan, and was a tribute student of the bingwu year.
Cui Yiyuan, Instructor in the Confucian School of Jishui County, Ji'an Prefecture, Jiangxi. His courtesy name was Ziren; he was from Lingchuan County, Guangxi, and was a tribute student of the gengzi year.
Zheng Gongfu, Instructor in the Confucian School of Dong'e County, Dongping Subprefecture, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong. His courtesy name was Changmao; he was from Changle County, Fujian, and was a tribute student of the gengzi year.
Li Chengchun, Instructor in the Confucian School of Wei County, Pingdu Subprefecture, Laizhou Prefecture, Shandong. His courtesy name was Ziyang; he was from Yishan County, Guangxi, and was a tribute student of the gengzi year.

Examination Oversight Official
Li Fengshi, Investigating Censor for the Huguang Circuit. His courtesy name was Huafu; he was from Dezhou Subprefecture, Shandong, and was a metropolitan graduate of the jiachen year.

第壹場

四書

巍巍乎其有成功也！煥乎其有文章！

溥博淵泉而時出之。溥博如天，淵泉如淵。見而民莫不敬，言而民莫不信，行而民莫不說。

夏曰校，殷曰序，周曰庠，學則三代共之，皆所以明人倫也。

易

庸言之信，庸行之謹，閑邪存其誠，善世而不伐，德博而化。

動靜不失其時，其道光明。

範圍天地之化而不過。

天地設位，聖人成能，人謀鬼謀，百姓與能。

書

以昭受上帝，天其申命用休。

其難其慎，惟和惟一。

貌曰恭，言曰從，視曰明，聽曰聰，思曰睿。恭
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

How lofty were his accomplishments! How splendid were his cultural achievements!

His virtue is all-embracing and vast, deep and inexhaustible as a spring, and he brings it forth at the proper times. All-embracing and vast, it resembles Heaven; deep and inexhaustible, it resembles an abyss. When he appears, none among the people fail to respect him; when he speaks, none fail to trust him; when he acts, none fail to be pleased.

Under the Xia they were called xiao; under the Yin, xu; under the Zhou, xiang. The term xue, “school,” was common to all three dynasties. All served to clarify human relationships.

Book of Changes

He is trustworthy in everyday speech and careful in everyday conduct. He guards against evil and preserves his sincerity. He benefits the world without boasting; his virtue is far-reaching and transforms others.

In movement and stillness, he never misses the proper time; his Way is radiant and clear.

He encompasses and regulates the transformations of Heaven and Earth without going beyond their bounds.

Heaven and Earth take their appointed places, and the sage brings their capacities to fulfillment. People deliberate, spirits are consulted, and the common people participate in these capacities.

Book of Documents

Thereby he illustriously receives the favor of the Lord on High; Heaven will renew its mandate with blessings.

Treat the task as difficult and approach it cautiously; be harmonious and single-minded.

Demeanor should be reverent; speech, compliant; sight, clear; hearing, keen; thought, discerning. Reverence …

…produces solemnity; compliance produces good order; clear sight produces discernment; keen hearing produces sound planning; penetrating thought produces sagacity.
Reverent were those above, discerning were those below; their light shone throughout the four quarters, and none failed to apply themselves diligently to virtue.

Book of Odes
How splendid his lambskin robe! How brilliant its three ornaments! That man is an outstanding worthy of the state.
May the noble lord live ten thousand years, fittingly blessed with lasting good fortune.
There is a curving hill, and a whirlwind comes from the south. The gracious and gentle noble lord comes to roam and sing, giving voice to his song.
His sagely reverence increased daily; his radiant approach to Heaven was unhurried. He revered the Lord on High.

Legal judgments 〔five items〕: Officials exceeding the time limit for taking up their posts; determining household status by the registers; offering sacrifices to deities included in the state sacrificial canon; military personnel and civilians arranging to bring lawsuits jointly [?]; weaving prohibited silk fabrics.
Third Session
Policy questions 〔five questions〕
Question: In the Way of the ancient emperors and kings, nothing was greater than reverence for Heaven and diligent care for the people. This can be seen in the praises recorded in the Book of Odes, the Book of Documents, and other writings. In the ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, many rulers were sages and wise men, and government attained flourishing greatness. Their reverence for Heaven and diligent care for the people followed the same standard throughout. In later ages, outstanding sovereigns and righteous rulers responded to their times and brought about good government. Although they did not attain the greatness of antiquity, can any be identified whose achievements approached it? We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao expelled the Mongol Yuan, pacified the realm, reverently received Heaven’s glorious mandate, and ruled over all regions, with reverence…

text:

頒其敬

皇上天縱聖哲運際中興體道盡制於前益光
郊壇耕籍之典
欽
天記頌之作
無逸豳風之記
穀祇蠶壇之賦農桑禁奢之
詔糶粟賑貸之
===
頌其敬
天勤民若未易殫述真足以揚
祖烈而軼隆古也可備舉而陳之與我
聖祖
皇上契古帝王傳授之道者其亦有所本與顧
諸士揄揚之用昭
帝德之大
問天人相與之際甚嚴然所以察其彝象
punctuated:
天勤民之實，載在《政要》諸書者，匹隆古而陋近代矣。列聖纘承，率循無替。至我皇上，天縱聖哲，運際中興，體道盡制於前，益光郊壇耕籍之典，欽天記頌之作，無逸豳風之記，穀祗蠶壇之賦，農桑禁奢之詔，藥粟賑貸之頒，其敬天勤民者，未易殫述，真足以揚祖烈而軼隆古也。可備舉而陳之與？我聖祖、皇上契古帝王傳授之道者，其亦有所本與？願諸士揄揚之，用昭帝德之大。
問：天人相與之際甚嚴，然所以察其垂象
translation_en:
…Heaven and diligently caring for the people: the actual deeds recorded in Essentials of Government (Zhengyao) and other books rival those of high antiquity and put more recent ages to shame. The successive sage emperors inherited this legacy and followed it without fail. Our present Emperor, endowed by Heaven with sagely wisdom, has come to the throne at a time of resurgence. Embodying the Way and fully establishing institutions beforehand [?], he has further brought distinction to the rites at the suburban sacrificial altars and the ceremonial ploughing of the imperial field; to the composition of records and eulogies on revering Heaven; to records concerning Against Idleness (Wuyi) and the Airs of Bin (Binfeng); to rhapsodies on the grain deity [?] and the Altar of Silkworms; to edicts promoting agriculture and sericulture and prohibiting extravagance; and to distributions of medicines and grain as relief and loans. His acts of revering Heaven and diligently caring for the people cannot readily be recounted in full. They truly suffice to exalt his ancestors’ achievements and surpass high antiquity. Can you enumerate and explain them comprehensively? In conforming to the Way transmitted by the ancient emperors and kings, do our sagely founding ancestor and our present Emperor likewise have a fundamental basis upon which they draw? We hope that you scholars will extol these achievements, thereby making manifest the greatness of imperial virtue.
Question: The interaction between Heaven and humanity is a matter of the utmost gravity. Yet the means by which one observes the signs Heaven displays…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
而驗其災祥者莫大於經星與七政也
經星體靜七政性殊曆象推測之數自
歷代固然其所稱有二十一家者亦能
盡其道與今姑自其疑者言之經星莫
大於紫宮均之連亘五星也而帝與后
宮占者錯雜或主孔子北辰之說斷之
果可信焉然與夫在天象五方在地象
五嶽二十八宿分四方似矣中獨無所
主與天體一定日行宜無所易而胡為
===
有歲差二曜並明月行宜同於日而胡
為有九道至若五緯獨有遲逆金水獨
不經天氣物紛紜機理茫昧所以鈎深
而玄契之者道當何所始也夫聖人法
天遇災而懼或以七政俱行黃道不能
無凌犯去不甚近者不可誇張為異以
啟不信之心是恐懼為虛與抑别有說
也諸士子學以達天固嘗究心於是矣
請明著于篇毋徒諉曰讖數不講也

請明著于篇毋徒諉曰讖數不講也
punctuated: 而驗其災祥者，莫大於經星與七政也。經星體靜，七政性殊，曆象推測之數，自歷代固然。其所稱有二十一家者，亦能盡其道與？今姑自其疑者言之。經星莫大於紫宮，均之連亘五星也，而帝與后宮占者錯雜，或主孔子北辰之說斷之，果可信焉？然與夫在天象五方，在地象五嶽，二十八宿分四方似矣，中獨無所主與？天體一定，日行宜無所易，而胡為有歲差？二曜並明，月行宜同於日，而胡為有九道？至若五緯獨有遲逆，金水獨不經天，氣物紛紜，機理茫昧，所以鈎深而玄契之者，道當何所始也？夫聖人法天，遇災而懼，或以七政俱行黃道，不能無凌犯，去不甚近者，不可誇張為異，以啟不信之心，是恐懼為虛與？抑别有說也？諸士子學以達天，固嘗究心於是矣。請明著于篇，毋徒諉曰讖數不講也。
translation_en:
…and for verifying the calamities and auspicious signs they portend, nothing is more important than the fixed stars and the Seven Luminaries—the sun, moon, and five planets. The fixed stars are stationary in their configuration, while the Seven Luminaries differ in their natures. Techniques for calculating and predicting celestial phenomena have certainly existed throughout successive dynasties. Yet can the so-called twenty-one schools fully comprehend their principles? Let us now discuss some points of uncertainty.

Among the fixed stars, none is more important than the Purple Palace. They are alike five stars extending in a connected array [?], yet the divinatory assignments to the emperor and the rear palace are intermingled. Some base their judgments on Confucius’s statement about the North Star: can this really be trusted? Furthermore, the twenty-eight lunar lodges, divided among the four quarters, seem to correspond to the five regions in heaven and the Five Sacred Peaks on earth; does the center alone have nothing presiding over it?

Since the celestial sphere is fixed, the sun’s course ought not to change; why, then, is there precession? The two luminaries shine together, and the moon’s course ought to be the same as the sun’s; why, then, does it have nine paths? As for the five planets, why do they alone slow down and move backward, and why do Venus and Mercury alone not traverse the heavens? Vital forces and material phenomena are bewilderingly diverse, and their workings and principles obscure. Where should one begin in seeking out their depths and attaining a profound understanding of them?

The sage takes Heaven as his model and responds to calamities with fear. Some, however, hold that because the Seven Luminaries all travel along the ecliptic, close approaches and encroachments cannot be avoided; where their separation is not particularly small, these events must not be exaggerated into anomalies, thereby giving rise to disbelief. Does this mean that such fear is groundless? Or is there another explanation? You candidates study in order to comprehend Heaven and surely have already examined these matters attentively. Please set out your understanding clearly in your essays; do not merely evade the issue by saying that prophetic and numerical arts are not subjects you study.

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
問設官分職以爲民也要在教養安全之
耳古稱盛治如唐虞三代果師牧武衛
之臣適當人才之盛與抑翕受敷施之
者有其機與嗣是而下英君誼辟所得
名世之臣豈無有可言者論守令者首
稱漢如潁川東郡扶風南陽之守吏治
蒸蒸顯於神爵五鳳之間論師儒者多
歸宋如濂洛關閩之賢上承道統符彼
五星奎聚之盛論將帥者多在孝武文
===
皇之時如出上谷出鴈門出代與隴西
能空龍城狼望之王庭如擊頡利擊吐
谷渾擊咄陸與高昌用收陰山瀚海之
圖版此其最著者他固未易枚舉也果
孰爲盛與然不能並蓄兼收如唐虞三
代者何與或謂當時之君各以意向作
人之故是則然矣我
皇上以文武中正之才孜孜於
聖神功化之治激厲臣工以教養安全之者

===
皇上以文武中正之才孜孜於
聖神功化之治激厲臣工以教養安全之者
punctuated: 問：設官分職以爲民也，要在教養安全之耳。古稱盛治，如唐虞三代，果師牧武衛之臣適當人才之盛與？抑翕受敷施之者有其機與？嗣是而下，英君誼辟所得名世之臣，豈無有可言者？論守令者首稱漢，如潁川、東郡、扶風、南陽之守，吏治蒸蒸，顯於神爵、五鳳之間。論師儒者多歸宋，如濂洛關閩之賢，上承道統，符彼五星奎聚之盛。論將帥者多在孝武、文皇之時，如出上谷、出鴈門、出代與隴西，能空龍城、狼望之王庭；如擊頡利、擊吐谷渾、擊咄陸與高昌，用收陰山、瀚海之圖版。此其最著者，他固未易枚舉也。果孰爲盛與？然不能並蓄兼收如唐虞三代者何與？或謂當時之君各以意向作人之故，是則然矣。我皇上以文武中正之才，孜孜於聖神功化之治，激厲臣工以教養安全之者
translation_en:
Question: Offices are established and duties apportioned for the sake of the people; the essential purpose is simply to instruct, nurture, secure, and protect them. Antiquity’s flourishing government is exemplified by the ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. Was it truly that the ministers who taught and shepherded the people and provided military protection happened to live amid an abundance of talent? Or did those who gathered and deployed them possess some effective means? In subsequent ages, surely there is something to be said of the ministers renowned in their times whom enlightened rulers and righteous sovereigns secured?

When discussing commandery governors and county magistrates, one first praises the Han. Such were the governors of Yingchuan, Dongjun, Fufeng, and Nanyang: their administration flourished, achieving distinction during the Shenjue and Wufeng reign periods. When discussing Confucian teachers, most give precedence to the Song. Such were the worthies of Lian, Luo, Guan, and Min, who inherited the transmission of the Way from earlier sages, fulfilling the auspicious portent of the five planets gathering in the Kui constellation. When discussing generals, most look to the times of Emperor Xiaowu of Han and Emperor Wen of Tang. Some marched out from Shanggu, Yanmen, Dai, and Longxi and were able to empty the royal courts at Longcheng and Langwang. Others attacked Jieli, Tuyuhun, Duolu, and Gaochang, thereby bringing the lands of Yinshan and Hanhai within the realm’s maps and registers. These are the most prominent examples; the others cannot readily be enumerated.

Which age, then, truly excelled? And why could none gather and employ all these kinds of talent together, as in the ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties? Some say this was because the rulers of those times each cultivated men according to their own inclinations. That is indeed so. Our August Sovereign, endowed with civil and military talents that are balanced and upright, diligently pursues government marked by sagely and divine achievements and transforming influence, exhorting his officials to instruct, nurture, secure, and protect the people …

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
未嘗有所軒輊誠唐虞三代之
盛心也何守令無善治學校無真儒封疆無
禦侮折衝之將帥果人才不逮無能奮
庸熈載與抑鼓舞作興之道有未盡與
爾多士有安攘之畧可以仰賛
明作於萬一者其毋訒於言
問立言之士或自創始或擬前人剛述而
後無慮數十卓然名家者亦不多得猶
不免後人之議然則立言不足以垂不
===
朽耶姑言世所傳者身為國史而述傳
以裨經蘭陵退處而纂言以翼聖放逐
摛詞用紓幽憤之懷網羅舊聞整齊世
傳之故所謂創始者也後人咸有譏言
何耶偏見荒言儒者弗道是矣至裨益
經史者亦加疵擿得無傷於刻耶前二
家書亦有可取否耶準易論語而作經
擬洙泗而著說倣丘明之體而成書模
春秋之筆而修史均擬前人者也後人

===

以裨經蘭陵退處而纂言以翼聖故逐
摛詞用紓幽憤之懷網羅舊聞整齊世
傳之故所謂創始者也後人咸有譏言

經史者亦加疵摘得無傷於刻耶前二
家書亦有可取否耶準易論語而作經
擬洙泗而著說倣丘明之體而成書模
春秋之筆而修史均擬前人者也後人
punctuated:
未嘗有所軒輊，誠唐虞三代之盛心也。何守令無善治，學校無真儒，封疆無禦侮折衝之將帥？果人才不逮，無能奮庸熈載與？抑鼓舞作興之道有未盡與？爾多士有安攘之畧，可以仰賛明作於萬一者，其毋訒於言。

問：立言之士，或自創始，或擬前人，剛述而後，無慮數十，卓然名家者亦不多得，猶不免後人之議。然則立言不足以垂不朽耶？姑言世所傳者：身為國史而述傳以裨經，蘭陵退處而纂言以翼聖，放逐摛詞用紓幽憤之懷，網羅舊聞整齊世傳之故，所謂創始者也。後人咸有譏言，何耶？偏見荒言，儒者弗道，是矣；至裨益經史者亦加疵擿，得無傷於刻耶？前二家書亦有可取否耶？準易論語而作經，擬洙泗而著說，倣丘明之體而成書，模春秋之筆而修史，均擬前人者也。後人
translation_en:
…has never favored one over the other. This is truly the lofty intention of the rulers of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. Why, then, do prefects and magistrates fail to govern well, schools lack true Confucian scholars, and the frontiers lack commanders who can repel aggression and overcome the enemy? Is talent truly inadequate, with none capable of exerting themselves in service and bringing distinction to their duties? Or have the means of encouraging and fostering talent not been fully realized? You assembled scholars, if you have strategies for securing peace within and repelling threats from without that might contribute even the slightest assistance to His Majesty’s enlightened endeavors, do not hesitate to speak.

Question: Among those who establish a legacy through writing, some originate their own works, while others imitate their predecessors. In the subsequent transmission of writings [?], they number in the dozens, yet few stand out as acknowledged masters, and even these do not escape criticism by later generations. Does this mean that writing is insufficient to secure immortality? Let us consider works transmitted to the present: one author, serving as a state historian, composed a commentary to supplement a classic; another, living in retirement in Lanling, compiled teachings to support the sage; another, banished, poured forth verse to relieve his hidden grief and indignation; another gathered accounts of the past and arranged the traditions handed down through the generations. These are what we call originators. Why have later generations criticized them all? It is proper that Confucian scholars should decline to speak of biased views and extravagant statements. But when faultfinding extends even to works that supplement the classics and histories, does it not become excessively harsh? Do the books of the former two authors also contain anything worth retaining?

Some composed a classic modeled on the Book of Changes and the Analects; some wrote expositions in imitation of the teachings associated with the Zhu and Si rivers; some compiled a book following Qiuming’s form; and some compiled a history modeling their brushwork on the Spring and Autumn Annals. All these imitated their predecessors. Later generations…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
或予或斥何耶覆瓿架屋君子信之宜
矣至以筆削自任者即尊爲不刊之典
得無近於諛耶此二賢書亦有得失可
言否耶願聞折衷之論
問治乆則弊生其生也有原弊釐則治復
其復也有道隆古遠矣近代漢稍近古
唐次之宋法制愈密論議愈詳似非漢
唐可及也夷考其實乃反有不逮者何
與豈質存者其治差勝文盛者其弊彌
===
深有固然與我
朝創制立法度越千古
皇上中興尤極振飭致治之美非近代可同語
也顧承平既乆玩愒易生
皇上赫然震曜痛釐時弊拔才恤困足食練兵
用建安攘之治不知有司之奉行者果
皆懋修實政以副
聖心之所期與抑或未盡然與夫治患不務實
耳乃務之而寡效其故安在誠欲捄之

唐可及也夷考其實乃反有不逮者何
與豈實存者其治差勝文盛者其弊彌
===
深有固然與我
朝創制立法度越千古
皇上中興尤極振飭致治之美非近代可同語
也顧承平既久玩愒易生
皇上赫然震曜痛釐時弊拔才恤困足食練兵
用建安攘之治不知有司之奉行者果
皆懋修實政以副
聖心之所期與抑或未盡然與夫治患不務實
耳乃務之而寡效其故安在誠欲捄之
punctuated:
或予或斥，何耶？覆瓿架屋，君子信之宜矣。至以筆削自任者，即尊爲不刊之典，得無近於諛耶？此二賢書亦有得失可言否耶？願聞折衷之論。
問：治乆則弊生，其生也有原；弊釐則治復，其復也有道。隆古遠矣，近代漢稍近古，唐次之。宋法制愈密，論議愈詳，似非漢唐可及也。夷考其實，乃反有不逮者，何與？豈質存者其治差勝，文盛者其弊彌深，有固然與？我朝創制立法，度越千古。皇上中興，尤極振飭，致治之美，非近代可同語也。顧承平既乆，玩愒易生。皇上赫然震曜，痛釐時弊，拔才恤困，足食練兵，用建安攘之治。不知有司之奉行者，果皆懋修實政，以副聖心之所期與？抑或未盡然與？夫治患不務實耳，乃務之而寡效，其故安在？誠欲捄之，
translation_en:
…why do some approve while others condemn? That such writings are fit to cover jars or merely pile up beneath the rafters—gentlemen may indeed reasonably accept these judgments. Yet when someone takes upon himself the task of editorial judgment, they immediately exalt his work as an unalterable canon: does this not approach flattery? Can the merits and shortcomings of the writings of these two worthies also be discussed? We wish to hear a balanced assessment.
Question: When good government has endured for a long time, abuses arise, and their emergence has its sources. When abuses are corrected, good government returns, and its restoration has its proper methods. High antiquity is distant. Among the more recent dynasties, the Han came somewhat close to antiquity, and the Tang ranked next. Under the Song, laws and institutions became ever more elaborate, and deliberations ever more detailed, seemingly beyond anything the Han and Tang could attain. Yet on examining the actual results, we find that in some respects the Song instead fell short. Why was this? Is it inherently the case that where substance survives, government is somewhat better, whereas where outward elaboration flourishes, abuses grow ever deeper? Our dynasty established institutions and laws surpassing those of all preceding ages. His Majesty, in bringing about a restoration, has exerted himself to the utmost to invigorate and rectify government. The excellence of the order he has achieved cannot be spoken of in the same terms as that of recent dynasties. Yet when peace has endured for a long time, negligence and idle delay readily arise. His Majesty has displayed his awe-inspiring authority, vigorously corrected current abuses, promoted talented men, relieved those in distress, ensured adequate provisions, and trained the troops, thereby establishing a government that secures peace within and repels threats from without. We do not know whether the responsible officials implementing these measures all diligently attend to practical governance so as to fulfill His Majesty’s expectations, or whether some have yet to do so fully. The trouble with government lies simply in failing to attend to practical realities; yet when these are attended to and results remain scant, where does the cause lie? If one truly wishes to remedy this…

Four Books

“How lofty were his achievements! How splendid were his cultural institutions!”

Fang Yourong

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: “In praising the flourishing government of Fangxun [Yao], this captures the meaning of Confucius’s words. An excellent examination essay.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Cui, Instructor: “It develops almost exhaustively the traces of the sage’s ordering of the world. Accept it.”

The sage takes the visible manifestations of the emperor’s government and praises their magnificence to the utmost, thereby revealing the greatness of his virtue. Achievements and cultural institutions are, indeed, the manifestations of Yao’s virtue in government. People can only look up in admiration at their magnificence; how could they give adequate expression to his virtue? Earlier, the Master praised the age of Tang and Yu [Yao and Shun], acclaiming Yao with the words “Great indeed!” Here, he seems to say: Yao’s virtue was so vast that it truly defied description. Yet could it ultimately vanish into nothingness, leaving no visible manifestation? title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
嘗稽堯之時盖巍巍乎其有成功也放勳之敷
世極充周而不窮大化之底績咸怙冒而無外
始於親睦終於協和用臻於變時雍之休者其
諸明俊之效也乎被于四表格于上下式昭發
育峻極之盛者其諸至治之迹也乎參天地以
並立合上下而同流巍巍乎何其高大也哉有
一代之興必有一代之制求其光明則寡矣吾
嘗稽唐之世盖煥乎其有文章也禮樂宣昭有
以闡人文之賁制度精明有以發物采之章顯
===
於朝廷之近施於邦國之遠經緯有章而幾微
悉著矣殆抑之而愈揚也鉅而曆象之察繁而
庶績之熈光輝宣著而昭明有融矣殆遏之而
愈光也並日月以為明極照臨而有燿煥乎何
其光明也哉是則治之顯於有象者其盛如此
此堯之粗迹也若夫德豈得而名之耶堯其鮮
儷也已抑成功文章與德非二也盖德者渾然
之體成功文章燦然之用然即其用之極盛而
其體之大益彰此堯之所以為大也夫堯之德

punctuated: 嘗稽堯之時，盖巍巍乎其有成功也！放勳之敷，世極充周而不窮；大化之底績，咸怙冒而無外。始於親睦，終於協和，用臻於變時雍之休者，其諸明俊之效也乎？被于四表，格于上下，式昭發育峻極之盛者，其諸至治之迹也乎？參天地以並立，合上下而同流，巍巍乎何其高大也哉！有一代之興，必有一代之制，求其光明則寡矣。吾嘗稽唐之世，盖煥乎其有文章也！禮樂宣昭，有以闡人文之賁；制度精明，有以發物采之章。顯於朝廷之近，施於邦國之遠，經緯有章而幾微悉著矣，殆抑之而愈揚也。鉅而曆象之察，繁而庶績之熈，光輝宣著而昭明有融矣，殆遏之而愈光也。並日月以為明，極照臨而有燿，煥乎何其光明也哉！是則治之顯於有象者，其盛如此，此堯之粗迹也。若夫德，豈得而名之耶？堯其鮮儷也已！抑成功文章與德非二也。盖德者渾然之體，成功文章燦然之用。然即其用之極盛，而其體之大益彰，此堯之所以為大也。夫堯之德
translation_en:
…have examined the age of Yao: how lofty were his accomplishments! His far-reaching achievements spread throughout the world, utterly comprehensive and inexhaustible; the accomplishments of his great transforming influence sheltered and protected all, leaving none outside. Beginning with affection and harmony among his kin and culminating in concord among the states, he attained the blessed condition in which the people were transformed and all lived in harmony. Was this not the effect of his discerning and promoting men of outstanding virtue and ability? His influence extended to the four outer limits and reached above and below, manifesting the full grandeur of his nurturing power and supreme height. Were these not the traces of perfect governance? Standing alongside Heaven and Earth as their equal, joining above and below in a common flow—how lofty, how supremely great!

Whenever a dynasty arises, it must have institutions of its own; yet few possess true brilliance. I have examined the age of Tang, Yao’s dynasty: how radiant were its cultural forms! Rites and music were clearly displayed, revealing the beauty of human culture; institutions and regulations were refined and clear, bringing forth the splendor of all things. Manifest nearby at court and extended to the distant states, their interwoven order was patterned, and even the subtlest details were fully apparent. It was as though the more one pressed them down, the higher they rose. In great matters, there was careful scrutiny of celestial movements and the calendar; amid manifold affairs, every undertaking flourished. Their radiance shone forth, their brightness was pervasive: it was as though the more one restrained them, the more brightly they shone. Matching the sun and moon in brilliance, casting their light to the furthest reaches—how radiant, how supremely luminous!

Such was the grandeur of his governance as manifested in perceptible forms. Yet these were merely the outward traces of Yao. As for his virtue, how could it be named? Yao surely had few equals! Nevertheless, his accomplishments and cultural forms were not separate from his virtue. Virtue is the undivided underlying substance; accomplishments and cultural forms are its resplendent functioning. Through the utmost flourishing of that functioning, the greatness of its underlying substance becomes still more manifest. This is what made Yao great. Now, as for Yao’s virtue…

translation_en:
…pushed to its utmost extent, it reaches even to matching Heaven; traced to its root, however, it begins with making virtue bright. And the single word “reverence” expresses the essential substance of the teaching of the mind. How could Yao have added anything beyond his innate nature? If students take Confucius’s words “Great indeed!” and consider them alongside Mencius’s account of the goodness of human nature, they will grasp this.

“All-embracing and vast, deep as a wellspring, he brings it forth at the proper time. All-embracing and vast as Heaven, deep as an abyss: when he appears, none among the people fails to respect him; when he speaks, none fails to trust him; when he acts, none fails to be pleased.”
Cao Bo 曹愽

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Instructor: His thought is refined and precise, and his language serene and harmonious. He seems to be someone who has investigated the Learning of Principle and gained understanding from it.
Comment by Associate Examiner Hu, Instructor: Most who write on this topic indulge in empty rhetoric and thereby depart from its fundamental meaning. This is the only essay I have seen whose language is concise and whose reasoning is clear.
Comment by Examiner Qin, Senior Compiler: Both expression and reasoning are fully accomplished.
Comment by Examiner Guo, Left Mentor: Grounded in the classics and substantial.

The Doctrine of the Mean sets forth how sagely virtue accumulates within and manifests itself outwardly, and further extols it. When both the inward and the outward attain their utmost fullness, this is virtue complete in both substance and function. Who but the utmost sage in the world could measure up to this? Zisi’s meaning is presumably that, where virtue lacks fullness, one can hardly speak of its substance; where its fullness has not reached the utmost, one can hardly speak of its function. Only the utmost sage in the world…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
也美質具乎生知純全妙乎天德吾知心體萃
衆善之極而虛受以盡其量周徧廣闊其溥博
矣乎本原涵萬化之端而資深以逢其原靜深
有本其淵泉矣乎其充積有如此者由是誠中
形外泛應獲曲當之妙元吉之履與時而偕行
也體信達順大用協時措之宜攸往之利圓神
而不滯也其發見有如此者不惟是也以言乎
溥博也含弘廣大而充周不窮如天之冲漠而
無朕也蓋有以冒天下之道矣以言乎淵泉也
===
渾淪停蓄而充滿無際如淵之幽深而莫測也
蓋有以統萬有之宗矣充積之盛若此非體極
其全者乎以言乎時出也彰法象於一身而示
顒觀于有衆時而見焉下觀而化民無有乎弗
敬也渙訓命于四方而敷猷為于天下時而言
且行焉不應徯志民無有乎弗信且悅也發見
之當可若此非用極其妙者乎此學問之極功
聖人之能事也聖德大業至矣哉雖然此豈有
異物哉溥博淵泉者所謂致中立天下之大本

translation_en:
…His excellent endowment is complete in his innate knowledge, and his purity and wholeness wondrously embody Heaven’s virtue. We know that the substance of his mind gathers all goodness in its utmost perfection, while its receptive emptiness realizes the full extent of its capacity. All-embracing and expansive—is this not his breadth and vastness! His fundamental source contains the beginnings of all transformations; drawing deeply upon it, he encounters its wellspring. Still, deep, and firmly rooted—is this not his depth as a fountain!

Such is the fullness accumulated within him. Hence his inner sincerity takes outward form. In responding to all things, he achieves the subtle perfection of fitting each particular circumstance; his conduct, supremely auspicious, advances together with the times. Embodying trustworthiness and bringing accord to realization, his great activity suits what is appropriate to each occasion. Beneficial wherever he proceeds, he is wondrously adaptable and unimpeded. Such are his outward manifestations; yet there is more.

To speak of his breadth and vastness: encompassing, capacious, and expansive, he fills all things without exhaustion, like Heaven’s empty stillness, without perceptible trace. Thus he possesses the Way that embraces all under Heaven. To speak of his depth as a fountain: an undivided whole, collected and stored, he is full without limit, like a pool whose secluded depths cannot be fathomed. Thus he possesses the source that unifies all existence. With such abundant fullness accumulated within, has not his underlying substance attained perfect completeness?

To speak of his coming forth at the proper time: he makes exemplary patterns manifest in his own person and presents himself for the multitude’s reverent contemplation. When he appears at the proper time, those below behold him and are transformed; none among the people fails to revere him. He disseminates instructions and commands throughout the four quarters and extends his plans and actions throughout the world. When he speaks and acts at the proper time, ‘without responding, they await his intent’ [?]; none among the people fails to trust him and rejoice. With outward manifestations so fitting, has not his functioning attained the utmost subtlety?

This is the ultimate achievement of learning and inquiry, the consummate accomplishment of the sage. How supreme are his sagely virtue and great undertakings! Yet could these be anything different? His breadth and vastness, his depth as a fountain, are what is meant by bringing centrality to its utmost and establishing the great foundation of all under Heaven…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
鄉論秀不可無學也若夏嘗取教民之義而名
曰校矣殷改爲序則有取於習射之義焉周改
爲庠則有取於養老之義焉隨時變易其不同
有如此者國都之中四方表率則以次升才不
可無學也若夏固謂之學而無異名矣繼夏而
殷名實因乎夏焉繼殷而周名亦因乎殷焉三
聖相承其不變有如此者夫鄉國異地也夏殷
周異時也導民之方豈或有求於恒性之外者
哉亦以五典在人雖燦然其同具也然行不著
===
而習不察者有矣非學何以明其理乎亦秩然
其有叙也然汩於私而溺於俗者有矣非教何
以通其蔽乎故於父子而明有親焉於君臣而
明有義焉所以聯師儒而申其義者其在鄉學
也猶其在國學者矣明其序於長幼也明其别
若信於夫婦朋友也所以群弟子而敬其業者
殷不能改乎夏周不能改乎殷矣否則何裨於
民而亦何取於教邪是不必同者其名也不容
異者其實也循名責實而教可興矣抑是道也

punctuated: 鄉論秀，不可無學也。若夏嘗取教民之義而名曰校矣，殷改爲序，則有取於習射之義焉；周改爲庠，則有取於養老之義焉。隨時變易，其不同有如此者。國都之中，四方表率，則以次升才，不可無學也。若夏固謂之學而無異名矣，繼夏而殷，名實因乎夏焉；繼殷而周，名亦因乎殷焉。三聖相承，其不變有如此者。夫鄉國異地也，夏殷周異時也，導民之方，豈或有求於恒性之外者哉？亦以五典在人，雖燦然其同具也，然行不著而習不察者有矣，非學何以明其理乎？亦秩然其有叙也，然汩於私而溺於俗者有矣，非教何以通其蔽乎？故於父子而明有親焉，於君臣而明有義焉，所以聯師儒而申其義者，其在鄉學也猶其在國學者矣。明其序於長幼也，明其别若信於夫婦朋友也，所以群弟子而敬其業者，殷不能改乎夏，周不能改乎殷矣。否則何裨於民，而亦何取於教邪？是不必同者其名也，不容異者其實也。循名責實而教可興矣。抑是道也，
translation_en:
…the local communities to assess outstanding talent: schools were indispensable. The Xia once took the meaning of instructing the people and named their schools jiao. The Yin changed the name to xu, drawing on the meaning of practicing archery; the Zhou changed it to xiang, drawing on the meaning of caring for the aged. Their names changed with the times: such were their differences. Within the royal capital, which set an example for all regions, schools were likewise indispensable for advancing talented men through successive stages. Under the Xia, these were simply called xue, with no other name. The Yin succeeded the Xia and followed the Xia in both name and substance; the Zhou succeeded the Yin and likewise followed the Yin in name. The three sage rulers succeeded one another: such was the continuity of what they left unchanged.

Now, local communities and the royal capital were different places, and the Xia, Yin, and Zhou were different ages. Yet could their methods of guiding the people ever have sought anything outside the constant human nature? The five norms of human relationships are manifestly possessed by everyone alike. Yet some act upon them without understanding them and practice them without examining them. Without learning, how could their principles be made clear? These relationships also have their orderly arrangement. Yet some are submerged in selfishness and engulfed by vulgar customs. Without instruction, how could their obstructions be cleared away? Thus, affection was made clear in the relationship between father and son, and righteousness in that between ruler and minister. In bringing together teachers and scholars to expound these principles, the local schools were just like the schools of the royal capital. They clarified precedence between elder and younger, distinctions between husband and wife, and trust between friends. In gathering pupils together and having them treat their studies with reverence, the Yin could not alter what the Xia had done, nor the Zhou what the Yin had done. Otherwise, what benefit would there have been for the people, and what value in instruction? Thus, what need not remain the same was the name; what could not differ was the substance. By examining the names and requiring the corresponding substance, instruction could flourish. Moreover, this Way…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
不可尚哉彼行不當者是謂妄動非時也惟時
行而行則感而遂通不失順應之常圓神无滯
適得妙用之顯其感其應固非憧憧往来之私
也動何至於失時耶止不當者是謂固滯非時
也惟時止而止則寂然不動而靜專之妙以凝
至靜无感而虛靈之性不爽无思无為乃其純
一不雜之真也靜何至於失時耶動不失其時
則動與道游而獲安貞之吉動而得所止矣靜
不失其時則靜與道俱而湛淵默之體靜而得
===
所止矣其道不亦光明矣乎盖動妄則邪謂之
光明不可也今動得其止則妄動俱息而百慮
皆融有以成天下之化靜滯則暗謂之光明則
未也今靜得其止則一真自如而萬理明淨有
以立天下之本靜虛而動直瑩然內外之澄徹
也篤實輝光之發自有不可掩者矣明通而公
溥燦然體用之宣著也昭明有融之盛盖有不
可遏者矣由是觀之君子之道靜焉而時固止
也動焉而時亦止也止无分於動靜顧時之何

punctuated: 不可尚哉？彼行不當者，是謂妄動，非時也。惟時行而行，則感而遂通，不失順應之常；圓神无滯，適得妙用之顯。其感其應，固非憧憧往来之私也，動何至於失時耶？止不當者，是謂固滯，非時也。惟時止而止，則寂然不動，而靜專之妙以凝；至靜无感，而虛靈之性不爽。无思无為，乃其純一不雜之真也，靜何至於失時耶？動不失其時，則動與道游，而獲安貞之吉，動而得所止矣；靜不失其時，則靜與道俱，而湛淵默之體，靜而得所止矣。其道不亦光明矣乎？盖動妄則邪，謂之光明，不可也。今動得其止，則妄動俱息，而百慮皆融，有以成天下之化。靜滯則暗，謂之光明，則未也。今靜得其止，則一真自如，而萬理明淨，有以立天下之本。靜虛而動直，瑩然內外之澄徹也；篤實輝光之發，自有不可掩者矣。明通而公溥，燦然體用之宣著也；昭明有融之盛，盖有不可遏者矣。由是觀之，君子之道，靜焉而時，固止也；動焉而時，亦止也。止无分於動靜，顧時之何
translation_en:
…could it fail to deserve esteem? To act when action is inappropriate is called reckless movement: it is untimely. Only by acting when it is time to act does one respond to a stimulus and thereby achieve thorough understanding, preserving the constant principle of responding compliantly. Spiritually rounded and unobstructed, one aptly manifests the wondrous workings of the Way. Such responsiveness is certainly no selfish, restless coming and going. How, then, could movement become untimely? To stop when stopping is inappropriate is called obstinate stagnation: it is untimely. Only by stopping when it is time to stop does one remain still and unmoving, allowing the wondrous concentration of stillness to become settled. In utmost stillness, untouched by stimuli, the empty and numinous nature remains unimpaired. Without thought or contrived action, one possesses the authentic condition of pure, unmixed unity. How, then, could stillness become untimely? When movement does not miss its proper time, one moves in company with the Way and obtains the good fortune of peaceful steadfastness: in movement, one has found the proper place to rest. When stillness does not miss its proper time, one rests together with the Way, and one's essential being becomes profoundly tranquil and silent: in stillness, one has found the proper place to rest. Is this Way not radiant and clear?

Reckless movement is deviant; it cannot be called radiant and clear. But when movement finds its proper resting place, all reckless impulses cease and the hundred deliberations become integrated, enabling one to accomplish the transformation of all under Heaven. Stagnant stillness is dark; it cannot yet be called radiant and clear. But when stillness finds its proper resting place, undivided authenticity abides naturally and the myriad principles become clear and pure, enabling one to establish the foundation of all under Heaven. Empty in stillness and upright in movement, one is luminously clear both within and without. The radiance issuing from solid sincerity is naturally impossible to conceal. Illuminating and penetrating, impartial and all-embracing, one brilliantly manifests both substance and function. Such abundant, expansive brightness surely cannot be restrained.

易之作也非聖人不能而不知聖人之於易不
可无作也當易之未作也兩儀判而清濁分動
靜消長之幾雖具夫吉凶之理而不能以自昭
卑高陳而上下位剛柔盈虛之運雖蘊夫進退
之端而不能以自顯聖人者出仰觀俯察既立
象以盡意造化屈伸之秘其闡於有形矣乎遠
稽近取復繫辭以盡言理數精微之妙其昭於

punctuated:
易之作也，非聖人不能，而不知聖人之於易，不可无作也。當易之未作也，兩儀判而清濁分，動靜消長之幾，雖具夫吉凶之理，而不能以自昭；卑高陳而上下位，剛柔盈虛之運，雖蘊夫進退之端，而不能以自顯。聖人者出，仰觀俯察，既立象以盡意，造化屈伸之秘，其闡於有形矣乎？遠稽近取，復繫辭以盡言，理數精微之妙，其昭於有象矣乎？是聖人之易，寔成乎天地之能矣。不然，天地之能，不幾於隱耶？

自易之既作也，凡民之愚，將行而有疑也，周爰咨謀，既以可否而決於人；其謀而未定也，稽於卜筮，復以成敗而謀於鬼。由是受命如嚮，炳幾以開其先，觀象玩占而趨避之不迷者，其擬議變化之權乎？質之无疑，前知以啟其衷，彰往察来而鼓舞之不倦者，其變通出入之利乎？是聖人之易，百姓亦得與其能矣。不然，百姓貿貿，其將何所之耶？是則聖人一易之作，有功於天地，有功於生民如此。參三才而一之，易之道其至矣哉！雖然，未易言也。
translation_en:
…the Changes could not have been composed by anyone but a sage, yet they do not understand that the sage could not leave the Changes unwritten. Before the Changes was composed, the two primal powers had separated, and the clear and turbid had divided. Although the incipient workings of movement and stillness, waning and growth, embodied the principles of good and ill fortune, they could not make themselves manifest. The low and high were arrayed, and above and below took their places. Although the cycles of firmness and yielding, fullness and emptiness, contained the beginnings of advance and retreat, they could not reveal themselves. Then the sage arose. Looking upward and examining below, he established images to express his meaning fully: were not the secrets of creation’s contraction and expansion thereby disclosed in visible form? Investigating what was distant and drawing upon what was near, he further appended statements to give full verbal expression: were not the subtle mysteries of principle and number thereby made manifest through images? Thus the sage’s Changes truly brought the capacities of Heaven and Earth to fulfillment. Otherwise, would those capacities not have remained all but hidden?

Once the Changes had been composed, ordinary people, in their ignorance, would consult widely when they were about to act but had doubts, first seeking a decision from other people about whether an action was acceptable. If their deliberations remained unsettled, they turned to divination by turtle shell and milfoil, further consulting the spirits about success or failure. Thus, upon receiving an inquiry, the Changes responds like an echo, illuminating the first stirrings of events to reveal what lies ahead. By contemplating its images and pondering its prognostications, people are not confused about what to pursue and what to avoid: is this not its power to enable deliberation and transformation? When consulted, it leaves no doubt; foreknowledge enlightens people’s hearts. By making the past clear and discerning what is to come, it inspires them to act without weariness: is this not the benefit of adapting to change, whether going forth or withdrawing? Thus, through the sage’s Changes, the common people too can share in the capacities of Heaven and Earth. Otherwise, bewildered as they are, where would they turn? Such are the sage’s contributions to Heaven and Earth and to the living people through composing this single work, the Changes. Bringing together the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—and uniting them, how consummate is the Way of the Changes! Yet this is not easily explained.

translation_en:
…Is not his meaning profound? The point is that the five activities of human beings are produced by Heaven’s Five Phases. Stored within, they constitute virtue; expressed outwardly, they constitute function. This distinction must be examined. Why is this so? Demeanor is the consolidation of vital essence, visibly forming an imposing outward presence [?]. To be reverent without being negligent—is this not the virtue of demeanor? Speech is the voice of the heart, and harmony and compliance are the source of its words and tone. To be accordant without being contrary—is this not the virtue of speech? The eyes govern seeing: steadfast vision, free of confusion, contains the capacity to illuminate all around, and its virtue is clarity. The ears govern hearing: utter receptivity enables them to respond, providing ample scope for sensitivity to the myriad phenomena, and their virtue is acuity. As for probing the hidden things of the world and fully comprehending their causes, investigating the incipient workings of the world and exhausting their secrets: this is what is called discernment. Herein lies the virtue of thought. Thus, wherever there is a thing, there is a norm; as soon as bodily form comes into being, virtue resides within it. Is not each wholly sufficient in itself?
When reverence takes outward form, every movement and expression accords with ritual propriety, inspiring awe and providing a model. Does not solemnity arise from reverence? When accordance becomes manifest, virtuous utterances are ordered, coherent, and pertinent. Does not order arise from accordance? Clarity illuminates the past and examines what is to come, comprehensively knowing the principles of things and affairs; thus clarity gives rise to wisdom. Acuity makes weighing and judging precise and apt, bringing the affairs of the world to fulfillment in all their particulars; thus acuity gives rise to sound planning. 主治為君虞之君則帝舜而德威德明之化行
焉故上焉者緝熙無間凝以淵默之微中正為
觀斂以肅雍之度瞻之而莫見其偏也測之而

懋敬官常各著其精白之德奮庸帝載莫掩夫

其不及焉耳。稽古有虞之治，不可審所尚邪？彼主治為君，虞之君則帝舜，而德威德明之化行焉。故上焉者緝熙無間，凝以淵默之微；中正為觀，斂以肅雍之度。瞻之而莫見其偏也，測之而莫得其際也，不亦穆穆其容矣乎？輔治為臣，虞之臣則三后，而恤功成功之政行焉。故下焉者懋敬官常，各著其精白之德；奮庸帝載，莫掩夫明作之休。抑之而愈揚也，遏之而愈光也，不亦明明其容矣乎？夫誠精之發既昭著乎君臣，而德輝之動遂旁通乎遐邇。將見萬邦感帝德之廣運，而鼓舞奮發之有機；四國順百辟之具瞻，而舍舊圖新之恐後。會其有極，歸其有極，敏德之速，若或相之而不能自已者矣；自易其惡，自至其中，不仁者遠，若或驅之而莫知其然者矣。是何也？惟皇降衷，民有恒性。彼罔中于信者，淪於習也；勤德于上者，感於化也。治果尚刑乎哉？

…only where it falls short. In examining the ancient government of Youyu, should we not scrutinize what it esteemed? The ruler presided over government: the ruler of Youyu was Emperor Shun, and his transforming influence operated through virtue’s awe and illumination. Thus, he who stood above continued without interruption to make his virtue shine, grounding it in the subtle depths of silent composure. He presented a model of balance and rectitude, governing his bearing with reverence and harmony. Look upon him, and no partiality could be seen; fathom him, and no limit could be found. Was his bearing not profoundly majestic? Ministers assisted in government: the ministers of Youyu were the Three Lords, and their administration devoted itself to their tasks and brought them to completion. Thus, those below diligently respected the regular duties of their offices, each displaying his pure and unsullied virtue. They exerted themselves in the emperor’s service, and nothing obscured the excellence of their enlightened achievements. The more they were pressed down, the higher they rose; the more they were restrained, the more brightly they shone. Was their bearing not radiantly illustrious?

Once the expression of pure sincerity had become manifest in ruler and ministers, the stirring radiance of their virtue spread everywhere, near and far. One would then see the myriad states moved by the far-reaching operation of the emperor’s virtue, finding an impetus to rejoice and exert themselves. The lands in all four directions would follow the example of the assembled lords, to whom all looked, fearing to lag behind in abandoning old ways and seeking renewal. Gathering around that supreme standard and returning to it, they would hasten toward virtue as though someone were helping them, unable to stop themselves. Of themselves they would change their evil ways; of themselves they would attain rectitude. Those lacking benevolence would become distant, as though someone were driving them away, without their knowing how it happened. Why was this? August Heaven bestowed an inner moral norm, and the people possess a constant nature. Those who fail to attain rectitude and sincerity have sunk into ingrained habits; those who strive for virtue under their superiors have responded to their transforming influence. Does government truly place punishment foremost?

In general, the sage’s mind is one with Heaven. Thus Heaven’s stern, life-destroying action is exercised only after the myriad things have been nurtured and brought to maturity; likewise, Shun’s auspicious punishments appear only after the Three Lords…

text:
所願於王者何如耶誠以端凝九五君子之身
固天地民物之主也其必保合太和而多歷年
所引之以受命之長乎垂拱穆清君子之居固
元后父母之位也其必滋培元氣而歷年有永
延之以綿長之祚乎上帝有以默相之鬼神有
以陰隲之於萬斯年而景命之僕夫何有終窮
耶精神日益完固也氣體日益貞彊也萬有千
歲而眉壽之綏夫何有紀極耶夫如是將見天
佑君德而申命之休維日不足者何廣遠也君

申錫無疆者何悠久也君子則萬年宜之而罔
戾啓之以昭明申之以高朗日新月盛而元吉
之履盖將與天地相爲終始者矣不有以宜其
遐福乎畀之以戩穀益之以罄宜川至松茂而

自此而宜哉是何也盖壽者福之本福者壽之
幹固相因之幾而亦自然之理也必如是而臣

translation_en:
…what do we wish for our king? Truly, standing dignified and composed in the sovereign’s place—the fifth, yang line—the princely lord is indeed master of the people and all things between Heaven and Earth. Surely he must preserve supreme harmony in its integrity and pass through many years, prolonging the duration of his heavenly mandate! Sitting with folded hands amid solemn purity, the princely lord indeed occupies the position of supreme sovereign and parent to his people. Surely he must nourish the primal vital force and endure through long years, extending his lasting blessings!

The Lord on High silently assists him; ghosts and spirits aid him unseen. For ten thousand years the glorious mandate attends him: how could there be any end or limit? His spirit grows daily more whole and firm; his bodily vitality grows daily more steadfast and strong. For ten thousand years and a thousand more, he enjoys the peace of venerable longevity: how could its span be measured or bounded?

Thus we shall see Heaven protect the ruler’s virtue. How vast and far-reaching are the blessings of its renewed mandate, for whose bestowal even every day is insufficient! The princely lord bears them all in his own person and is worthy of them all. Heaven’s mandate descends under its watchful gaze. How enduring are the abundant blessings bestowed repeatedly without limit! For ten thousand years the princely lord remains worthy of them, without transgression. They begin with shining brightness and are renewed with lofty radiance. Renewed daily and flourishing monthly, his course of supreme good fortune will surely endure through beginnings and endings together with Heaven and Earth. Does this not make him worthy of those far-reaching blessings? He is granted happiness and goodness, and receives in addition everything fitting. Like rivers flowing toward him and pine trees flourishing, the felicity of great abundance will surely endure as long as the ruler himself. Is it not through this that he becomes worthy of far-reaching blessings?

translation_en:
… skilled in praise and prayer? I have reflected on the poem Wild Ducks and Gulls (Fu yi). Although it consists of a Zhou minister’s words praising his ruler, one can discern in it the principles governing Heaven and humanity and the duties binding superiors and subordinates. Heaven’s generous protection of the ruler is no private favoritism: it preserves his person and enables his rule to endure. A minister’s prayers and praise for his ruler are no excessive flattery: he relies upon the ruler’s virtue and wishes his beneficence to last. The ruler’s reverence for virtue, through which he wins Heaven’s favor, and his extension of blessings to those below—the subtle workings by which solicitude is elicited, and the sentiments of benevolence, generosity, loyalty, and love—abundantly manifest themselves beyond the words themselves. Commentators say that the vital breath of supreme harmony filled the world of Zhou in its flourishing days. How true!

“There is a winding hill; a whirlwind comes from the south. The gracious and amiable lord comes to roam and comes to sing, to give forth his song.”
Yang Jiujing

Associate Examiner Zhang, Professor, comments: “In framing his ideas and choosing his words, he displays outstanding judgment and proportion. He can indeed compose essays.”

Examiner Qin, Senior Compiler, comments: “He captures the loyal affection of the veteran minister.”

Examiner Guo, Left Secretariat Supervisor, comments: “Clear and clean.”

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
大臣於君因其豫樂而致賡歌之意焉甚矣古
人善導其君也一游歌之頃而即賡以寓戒忠
愛何其至哉昔周之盛時召康公從成王遊於
卷阿之上因作詩以陳戒其意蓋曰致天下之
治者固當克慎厥始而享天下之樂者亦宜圖
惟厥終吾王今日之游豈尋常者可擬哉大阿
卷曲協陰陽向背之宜蔚然竒勝之區也地之
可樂何以尚之飄風南來順歲功長養之候熈
然景物之會也時之可樂夫孰加焉我豈弟君
===
子也當熈洽之期而履盈成之運撫庶事之康
而值萬幾之暇駕言出遊翺翔於卷阿之上從
容休豫式暢夫昭曠之懷也歌以永言嘯咏于
飄風之前抑揚高下式振夫和平之音也宇宙
太和之會蓋千載之一時君臣喜起之風幸于
今之再見奭於斯時寧能已於言邪感治忽循
環之理而慶豫亨之方來因王之歌而載賡其
音庶幾一倡和之間而保治微指揄揚於篇章
之内矣乎思盛衰倚伏之幾而欣泰道之方亨

translation_en:
A great minister, attending upon his ruler, takes the occasion of the ruler’s recreation and enjoyment to convey his intentions through a song in response. How skillfully the ancients guided their rulers! In the brief span of an excursion and a song, they would at once respond with verses embodying admonition. How consummate their loyalty and affection!

Formerly, in Zhou’s flourishing days, Duke Kang of Shao accompanied King Cheng on an excursion to Juan’a and composed a poem to offer admonition. Its meaning was roughly this: one who brings order to All under Heaven must indeed exercise care at the outset; one who enjoys the pleasures of All under Heaven should likewise take thought for the end. How could any ordinary excursion compare with our king’s outing today? The great hillside curves and winds, its sunny and shaded aspects fittingly disposed: a magnificent place of extraordinary beauty. What could surpass the pleasures of this setting? A whirling wind comes from the south, in keeping with the season of growth and nurture that brings the year’s work to fruition: a radiant convergence of scenery and living things. What could exceed the pleasures of this time?

Our gracious and joyous lord, living in an age of flourishing concord and enjoying an era of fullness and accomplishment, oversees the well-being of all affairs and finds leisure amid the myriad concerns of government. He sets out in his carriage, roaming freely over Juan’a, at ease in his recreation, thereby giving free expression to his bright and expansive heart. He sings to prolong his words, chanting before the whirling wind; his voice rises and falls, sounding forth the tones of peace and harmony. Such a convergence of supreme harmony throughout the universe comes but once in a thousand years. We are fortunate to witness once more today that spirit in which ruler and ministers joyfully rouse one another to action. At such a time, how could I, Shi, refrain from speaking?

Moved by the principle that order and disorder recur in cycles, and rejoicing that ease and prosperity are now arriving, I follow the king’s song and respond to its music. Might it be that, in this exchange of song and response, the subtle purport of preserving good order will find expression within the verses? Reflecting on the incipient workings by which flourishing and decline depend upon and lie concealed within each other, and delighted that the way of peace is now prospering…

translation_en:
…Continuing the king’s song and presenting further verses, might he, in that brief exchange of response and praise, silently convey beyond words and their expressed meaning the enduring plan for bringing the undertaking to a worthy conclusion? Ah! The pleasure of roaming and singing had scarcely begun before words of admonition followed. One such as Duke Kang may indeed be said to have mastered the way of assisting a ruler by “introducing restrained counsel through the window.”
Moreover, Zhou was then flourishing, and King Cheng was an excellent ruler who preserved the achievements he had inherited. In composing “Winding Hills” (Juan a), the Duke of Shao elaborated upon the abundance of longevity, blessings, and emoluments to display the splendor of an age of good government. He followed this with counsels on cultivating virtue and employing worthy men, thereby embedding admonitions about preserving that good government. Was this because the times still gave cause for apprehension and the sovereign’s performance still required correction? Rather, such are the profound and far-reaching concerns of a seasoned elder who sets government right and assists an enlightened ruler. This is why King Cheng continued the excellence of Kings Wen and Wu, and why the Duke of Shao is named alongside the Duke of Zhou. When later generations recite “Winding Hills,” they can envision the flourishing partnership of ruler and ministers in that age.
Spring and Autumn Annals

“In summer, the Viscount of Xiao Zhu came to pay court.” Seventh year of Duke Xi.

text:
春秋於諸侯有斥其罪之黜於王者有表其爵
之陟於王者盖賞罰王者之大權也名衛朔而
爵黎来聖人有深意乎朔者何衛宣之子也怙
寵爭國周乃舉黔牟於位而廢之春秋於奔齊
而必斥以名者若曰討罪之典屬之司寇天子
所以懲天下也矧朔之構禍斁倫自干天憲尤
法所不赦者哉今而革其不順俾自絕乎康叔
之籍則足以洩輿情之憤而罪用丕懲者矣雖
曰復歸得國莫能禁其終也然同惡相濟由於

来之爵也傾心內附周乃從齊桓之請而進之
春秋於朝魯而遂稱以子者若曰命德之典掌
之宗伯天子所以勸天下也矧黎来之去逆効
順通好中華尤善所宜與者哉今而錫之爵號
俾內列乎五等之班則足以廣自新之路而善
用丕勸者矣雖曰故習之陋不能强而同也然
內夏外夷在於既往則然耳維新之命果誰得

translation_en:
In its treatment of the feudal lords, the Spring and Autumn Annals exposes the offenses of those demoted by the king and displays the ranks of those promoted by the king. For rewards and punishments are the king’s great prerogatives. In naming Shuo of Wei but giving Lilai his noble title, did the Sage have a profound intention? Who was Shuo? He was the son of Duke Xuan of Wei. Relying on favor, he contested possession of the state; the Zhou court therefore raised Qianmou to the throne and deposed him. When recording his flight to Qi, the Spring and Autumn Annals insists on reproving him by using his personal name. It is as though it says: the statutes for punishing offenses are entrusted to the Minister of Justice, and through them the Son of Heaven chastens all under Heaven. How much more so in Shuo’s case! He fomented disaster, subverted proper human relationships, and brought himself into conflict with Heaven’s laws—offenses that the law especially could not pardon. By now stripping him of his standing for his disobedience and letting him cut himself off from the register of Kangshu’s descendants, public indignation could be assuaged and wrongdoing severely punished. Although he returned and recovered the state, and no one could ultimately prevent it, this mutual assistance among partners in evil resulted merely from the failure of the five states to act as subjects. Who could actually abrogate the law of the universal king? Otherwise, it is the established rule that feudal lords are not called by their personal names while alive; why, then, was this consideration withheld from Shuo?

Who was the Viscount of Xiaozhu? This was the noble title of Lilai of Ni. He wholeheartedly submitted to the royal realm, and the Zhou court accordingly granted Duke Huan of Qi’s request and advanced him in rank. When recording his court visit to Lu, the Spring and Autumn Annals consequently calls him viscount. It is as though it says: the statutes for honoring virtue are administered by the Minister of Rites, and through them the Son of Heaven encourages all under Heaven. How much more so in Lilai’s case! He abandoned defiance, demonstrated obedience, and established friendly relations with the central states—good conduct especially deserving of recognition. By now bestowing a noble title upon him and admitting him to the five ranks of nobility, the path to self-renewal could be broadened and goodness greatly encouraged. Although the coarseness of old customs could not be forcibly made uniform with those of the central states, treating the Xia as insiders and the Yi as outsiders applied only to his former circumstances. translation_en:
…and efface it? Otherwise, it is also the established practice to record dependent rulers of the Yi and Di by personal name; why, then, accord this distinction to Li Lai? Thus, when punishment executes Heaven’s chastisement, evil can be checked; when rewards convey Heaven’s mandate, goodness can be encouraged. Supreme authority will then suffer no decline. This is the sage’s intention in honoring Zhou. For only the sovereign may wield punitive power, and only the sovereign may bestow blessings: not the slightest usurpation or deviation is permissible. Had the regional lords of that time taken to heart their role as protective bulwarks and ensured that supreme authority over rewards and punishments rested entirely with their ruler, Zhou would surely have revived. Admirable indeed was Duke Huan of Qi’s command to the regional lords: “Let no enfeoffment be made without reporting it.” In petitioning on behalf of Xiao Zhu, he was surely putting his own injunction into practice! As for the five states’ defiance of the royal command and support for Shuo, their offense was not merely against Zhou.
The men of Chu attacked Xu. In the third month, the duke met with the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, and the Earl of Cao to conclude a covenant at Muqiu. They then encamped at Kuang. Gongsun Ao led an army and joined the grand masters of the regional lords in relieving Xu. 〔Fifteenth year of Duke Xi〕
He Zishou.

Examiner Guo, Left Mentor, comments: “Refined and meticulous.”
The Spring and Autumn Annals records aggression by an outside power and severely censures the failure of the hegemon’s relief effort. This relief of Xu by Duke Huan of Qi…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之怠於至誠無息之道有間矣覇業所爲卑乎
且楚都于郢徐在山東一旦以徐即齊之故越
諸國而伐之是謂非義加人凌弱暴寡楚罪大
矣然以徐之密邇齊封桓且主盟中國者也於
門庭利禦之寇而無餽糧越險之難當何如焉
拯救哉顧乃二三其德謀弗協于衆心以友邦
之君而猶待於牡丘之盟安在其戮力同心以
濟天下之急也愛克厥威令弗飭于有衆以攘
卻之舉而復有于匡之次安在其整軍經武以
===
振中國之威也夫既盟而次事已悖矣使諸君
親將大衆悉行則楚氛可熄庶幾桑榆之收乎
而復宴安是懷弗躬弗親以倒懸之急徐遣大
夫往焉則是内存養寇之志外示恤患之名何
損於楚何裨於徐勤安攘之義者不如是也噫
至誠無息帝王之道也謹始慮卒亦春秋之教
也若桓之志義勇爲一匡大業終有是焉豈敦
不息而謹始卒之謂哉故書盟書次書大夫帥
師而桓之罪自見矣大抵業之久暫心之邪正

之怠於至誠無息之道有間矣霸業所爲卑乎

punctuated: 之怠於至誠無息之道有間矣，覇業所爲卑乎！且楚都于郢，徐在山東，一旦以徐即齊之故，越諸國而伐之，是謂非義加人，凌弱暴寡，楚罪大矣。然以徐之密邇齊封，桓且主盟中國者也，於門庭利禦之寇，而無餽糧越險之難，當何如焉拯救哉？顧乃二三其德，謀弗協于衆心，以友邦之君而猶待於牡丘之盟，安在其戮力同心以濟天下之急也？愛克厥威，令弗飭于有衆，以攘卻之舉而復有于匡之次，安在其整軍經武以振中國之威也？夫既盟而次，事已悖矣。使諸君親將大衆悉行，則楚氛可熄，庶幾桑榆之收乎！而復宴安是懷，弗躬弗親，以倒懸之急，徐遣大夫往焉，則是内存養寇之志，外示恤患之名。何損於楚？何裨於徐？勤安攘之義者不如是也。噫！至誠無息，帝王之道也；謹始慮卒，亦春秋之教也。若桓之志義勇爲，一匡大業，終有是焉，豈敦不息而謹始卒之謂哉？故書盟，書次，書大夫帥師，而桓之罪自見矣。大抵業之久暫，心之邪正……
translation_en:
…his negligence fell short of the Way of utmost sincerity maintained without cease. Is this not why the achievement of a hegemon is inferior? Chu had its capital at Ying, while Xu lay east of the mountains. Simply because Xu had aligned itself with Qi, Chu suddenly crossed the territories of several states to attack it. This was to inflict injustice upon others, oppress the weak, and brutalize the few: Chu’s guilt was great indeed. Yet Xu lay very close to Qi’s borders, and Duke Huan presided over the covenants of the central states. With an enemy at his doorstep, readily opposed, and without the difficulty of transporting provisions across dangerous terrain, how should he have gone to Xu’s rescue?

Instead, he wavered in his resolve, and his plans failed to unite the hearts of the others. Even with the rulers of friendly states, he still had to await the covenant at Muqiu. Where was his effort to join strength and purpose in relieving the urgent distress of All-under-Heaven? Indulgence overcame his authority, and his commands were not firmly enforced among his followers. An undertaking to repel the enemy was followed by a halt at Kuang. Where was his ordering of the armies and preparation for war to assert the might of the central states?

To halt after making the covenant was already a perverse course of action. Had the rulers all advanced, each personally leading his full forces, Chu’s threatening presence could have been dispelled. Perhaps something might still have been salvaged at the close of the day! Instead, they again cherished ease and comfort and would not act in person. Though the emergency was as desperate as being suspended upside down, they leisurely dispatched their grandees to the rescue. Thus, inwardly they harbored an intention to let the enemy grow, while outwardly claiming the credit for relieving distress. What harm did this do to Chu? What benefit did it bring Xu? Those who diligently fulfill the duty of securing the states and repelling invaders do not act this way.

Alas! Utmost sincerity maintained without cease is the Way of the emperors and kings. To be careful at the beginning and mindful of the end is also the teaching of the Spring and Autumn Annals. Duke Huan aspired to righteousness and acted courageously, achieving the great work of bringing the realm into order; yet he ended in conduct such as this. Could this be called steadfast perseverance and care for both beginning and end? Thus the Annals records the covenant, records the halt, and records the grandees leading the armies, and Duke Huan’s guilt becomes apparent of itself. In general, whether an undertaking endures or proves short-lived, whether the heart is perverse or upright…

…bring this about. Hegemons borrow benevolence and righteousness to gratify their private desires for profit. Thus, once their desires are satisfied, they become indolent and perfunctory, no longer capable of accomplishing anything. Long ago, Bo Yi admonished Shun: “Be neither idle nor neglectful.” This is the essential teaching on cultivating the mind transmitted from sage to sage through the ages. Had Duke Huan understood this, then, having borrowed these virtues for so long without returning them, how could one know that he did not truly possess them? Guan Zhong and the others cannot escape responsibility for his failure.

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之其尊又何如也位尊者易怠安保其政無廢
弛乎諸侯之權重而方伯得以制馭之其重又
何如也權重者易驕能保其勢無跋扈乎故必
遣王朝之大夫爲方伯之三監以位則方伯尊
而大夫卑大夫既不敢肆以權則大夫內而方
伯外方伯又不敢專威福之柄方伯司之大夫
從而糾覈之雖不禁其所行而亦不縱其所行
也廢置之事方伯主之大夫從而督察之雖不
制其所事而亦不任其所事也然是官也豈漫
===
===
無定數者哉以一州言之必以三人焉而爲一
定之制以八州言之皆以三人焉而無多寡之
殊儉於三人者所以專其責任使權不至於分
也否則其職既冗糾覈之者有異心矣豈可以
過乎必以三人者所以協其事權使政有所參
決也否則其事必攝督察之者有遺職矣豈可
以不及乎夫國有三監內外之相統也監以大
夫大小之相維也先王之世久安長治者以此
抑論三監之設固所以統諸侯之國矣然相制

夫大小之相維也先王之世久安長治者以此
抑論三監之設固所以統諸侯之國矣然相制
punctuated:
之，其尊又何如也？位尊者易怠，安保其政無廢弛乎？諸侯之權重，而方伯得以制馭之，其重又何如也？權重者易驕，能保其勢無跋扈乎？故必遣王朝之大夫爲方伯之三監。以位則方伯尊而大夫卑，大夫既不敢肆；以權則大夫內而方伯外，方伯又不敢專。威福之柄，方伯司之，大夫從而糾覈之，雖不禁其所行，而亦不縱其所行也。廢置之事，方伯主之，大夫從而督察之，雖不制其所事，而亦不任其所事也。然是官也，豈漫無定數者哉？以一州言之，必以三人焉，而爲一定之制；以八州言之，皆以三人焉，而無多寡之殊。儉於三人者，所以專其責任，使權不至於分也。否則其職既冗，糾覈之者有異心矣，豈可以過乎？必以三人者，所以協其事權，使政有所參決也。否則其事必攝，督察之者有遺職矣，豈可以不及乎？夫國有三監，內外之相統也；監以大夫，大小之相維也。先王之世久安長治者以此。

抑論三監之設，固所以統諸侯之國矣，然相制
translation_en:
…them: how much more exalted, then, is his own standing? Those of exalted standing easily grow negligent; how can one ensure that their administration will not fall into neglect? The feudal lords wield great power, yet the regional chief can control them: how much greater, then, is his own power? Those with great power easily grow arrogant; can one ensure that they will not wield it in defiance of authority? Thus grand masters of the royal court must be dispatched to serve as the three overseers of the regional chief. In rank, the regional chief is exalted and the grand masters subordinate, so the grand masters dare not act without restraint. In authority, the grand masters belong to the central court and the regional chief to the outer domains, so the regional chief in turn dares not act arbitrarily. The regional chief holds the power of punishment and reward, while the grand masters scrutinize and investigate his exercise of it. Although they do not prohibit his actions, neither do they give him free rein. The regional chief directs dismissals and appointments, while the grand masters supervise and inspect these matters. Although they do not dictate his conduct of affairs, neither do they leave it entirely to his discretion. Could the number of these officials, then, have been left unspecified? For a single province, there must be three men: this is a fixed institution. Across the eight provinces, each has three men, with no variation in number. Limiting the number to three concentrates their responsibility and prevents authority from becoming divided. Otherwise, the offices would become redundant, and those conducting scrutiny and investigation would pursue divergent aims. How could the number be exceeded? Requiring three men coordinates their authority over affairs and allows administrative decisions to be made through consultation. Otherwise, their duties would have to be performed by substitutes [?], and those charged with supervision and inspection would leave responsibilities unfulfilled. How could the number fall short? That the domains have three overseers ensures coordination between the central court and the outer domains; that grand masters serve as overseers ensures mutual support between the greater and lesser authorities. It was by these means that the age of the former kings enjoyed enduring peace and lasting good government.

今夫天以陰陽五行化生萬物，流行賦予，衆所同也。人得天地之氣以生，降衷秉彝，衆所同也。自夫氣稟之偏、物欲之蔽、習俗之染也，而衆人之視聖人始懸絶矣。聖人者，亦非加於性分之外也。清明在躬，志氣如神，性以御情，道以貞行，理以制欲，如斯而已矣。動而世為天下道，行而世為天下法，言而世為天下則，裁成輔相之道，綏來動和之化，固天下後世所賴以生生而敏德者也。若堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之為君，周公之為臣，孔子之為師，數聖人者，其選也。豈獨夷、惠也哉！

…trust would be lacking, and their moral influence would thus disappear: how could it move others? To speak of being moved is to speak of the subtle incipient impulse; to speak of moral influence is to speak of its spiritual efficacy; to speak of trust is to speak of sincerity. Because the impulse is subtle, it elicits a response; because the efficacy is spiritual, it acts swiftly; because the sincerity is real, it endures. If what is handed down does not endure, what is communicated does not arrive swiftly, and what touches others elicits no response, it is insufficient to exemplify the utmost attainment of sagehood. The sage’s mind is wholly aligned with principle, and his conduct accords with the Way; sincerity makes his power to move others worthy of trust. Though he himself passes away, the Way does not perish with him. Embodying the Way in his own person, he leaves a moral influence for a hundred generations, still powerful enough to stir prevailing customs and change their direction. Could his transforming instruction be slight? Mencius said, “The sage is the teacher of a hundred generations,” and applied this to Bo Yi and Liu Xiahui. His meaning was presumably of this kind.

Now Heaven, through yin and yang and the Five Phases, transforms and generates the myriad things; its circulating forces and endowments are shared by all. Human beings receive the vital energy of Heaven and Earth and thereby come into being; the inner moral nature bestowed upon them and the constant norms they uphold are shared by all. Only because of imbalances in their endowment of vital energy, obscuration by material desires, and contamination by habitual customs do ordinary people become so widely separated from sages. Yet the sage adds nothing beyond what belongs to his inherent nature. Clarity and discernment reside in his person, and his resolve and vital energy are spiritually efficacious. He uses his nature to govern his emotions, the Way to make his conduct upright, and principle to restrain his desires. That is all. When he acts, he serves for generations as a guide to all under Heaven; when he conducts himself, he serves for generations as their model; when he speaks, he serves for generations as their standard. His Way gives proper form to and assists the workings of Heaven and Earth; his transforming influence brings peace, draws people near, stirs them, and harmonizes them. These are indeed what all under Heaven and later generations depend upon to sustain life continually and diligently cultivate virtue. Such sages as Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu as rulers, the Duke of Zhou as a minister, and Confucius as a teacher are the foremost among them. How could this apply only to Bo Yi and Liu Xiahui?

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
稱夷惠者舉其偏以槩其全也堯舜禹湯文武
周公孔子皆全體之聖夷惠者得其偏而造其
極者也夫以其造其極也故可謂之聖以其得
之偏也故不可謂之全然其制行之高流風之
遠足以範後世而激頹俗也故曰聖人百世之
師也伯夷柳下惠是也夫二子者何以謂之聖
也伯夷聖之清者也柳下惠聖之和也清非離
世絕俗而和非同流合汙者也非其君不事非
其民不使治進亂退不屑於就者伯夷與不羞
汙君不卑小官進不隱賢必以其道不屑於去
者柳下惠與是皆合乎天理之正即乎人心之
安煥乎日月以為明而非耀也巍乎泰華以為
高而非亢也廓乎江海以為容而非濫也粹乎
金玉以為純而非飾也非聖人而能然乎哉其
使後世之興起者何也夫氣質易偏也物欲易
蔽也習俗易汙也使有聖人在上躬行教化倡
其從裁成輔相翼其行綏來動和鼓其趨人將
自易其惡自至其中安有所謂頑懦薄鄙者而
