punctuated:
稱夷惠者，舉其偏以槩其全也。堯舜禹湯文武周公孔子，皆全體之聖；夷惠者，得其偏而造其極者也。夫以其造其極也，故可謂之聖；以其得之偏也，故不可謂之全。然其制行之高、流風之遠，足以範後世而激頹俗也。故曰：「聖人，百世之師也，伯夷、柳下惠是也。」

夫二子者，何以謂之聖也？伯夷，聖之清者也；柳下惠，聖之和也。清非離世絕俗，而和非同流合汙者也。非其君不事，非其民不使，治進亂退，不屑於就者，伯夷與？不羞汙君，不卑小官，進不隱賢，必以其道，不屑於去者，柳下惠與？是皆合乎天理之正，即乎人心之安。煥乎日月以為明而非耀也，巍乎泰華以為高而非亢也，廓乎江海以為容而非濫也，粹乎金玉以為純而非飾也。非聖人而能然乎哉？

其使後世之興起者何也？夫氣質易偏也，物欲易蔽也，習俗易汙也。使有聖人在上，躬行教化倡其從，裁成輔相翼其行，綏來動和鼓其趨，人將自易其惡，自至其中，安有所謂頑懦薄鄙者而
translation_en:
To cite Bo Yi and Liu Xiahui is to take their particular attainments as illustrative of sagehood as a whole. Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius were all sages in the fullest sense; Bo Yi and Liu Xiahui attained one particular aspect and carried it to its utmost perfection. Because they carried it to its utmost perfection, they may be called sages; because their attainment was confined to one aspect, they cannot be called complete. Yet the loftiness of their conduct and the enduring reach of their influence suffice to set a standard for later generations and rouse a society whose customs have declined. Hence it is said: “Sages are the teachers of a hundred generations: Bo Yi and Liu Xiahui were such men.”

Why may these two men be called sages? Bo Yi was the pure among sages; Liu Xiahui was the harmonious among sages. Purity does not mean withdrawing from the world and severing ties with society, nor does harmony mean drifting with the crowd and sharing in its corruption. He would serve only a ruler whom he deemed fit to serve and employ only people whom he deemed fit to employ; he advanced in times of order and withdrew in times of disorder, disdaining to take up office. Was this not Bo Yi? He felt no shame in serving a corrupt ruler and did not regard a minor office as beneath him; upon entering service, he did not conceal his worth and invariably acted according to his Way, disdaining to depart. Was this not Liu Xiahui? Both accorded with the rectitude of Heaven’s principle and with what brings peace to the human heart. They shone like the sun and moon, giving light without ostentation; they towered like Mount Tai and Mount Hua, lofty without arrogance; they were expansive like rivers and seas, capacious without excess; they were refined like gold and jade, pure without embellishment. Could anyone but a sage be like this?

How is it that they inspire later generations to rise to moral endeavor? One’s psychophysical disposition readily becomes one-sided; material desires readily obscure one’s understanding; customary habits readily corrupt one. If a sage occupied the position above, personally practicing moral instruction to lead people to follow, shaping and assisting their development to support their conduct, and comforting them, drawing them near, stirring them, and bringing them into harmony to encourage their progress, people would of themselves reform their faults and attain the mean. How could there then be any of those called obstinate, timid, ungenerous, or narrow-minded who …

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
必俟夫聞風興起也邪惟聖人不常有也而人
不能皆自振拔而有為由是頑夫遠於廉懦夫
遠於立薄夫遠於敦鄙夫遠於寬拘於偏與蔽
而莫反錮於習而罔覺者衆也然本心之明未
息同具之理尚存不有以倡之孰從而随之不
有以啓之孰從而明之幸而百世之上聖人之
風猶傳而弗泯也則人之仰焉而思恍焉而喻
翕然而變者惡能已哉是故興起于清則頑可
使廉而懦可使立矣興起于和則薄可使敦而
===
鄙可使寬矣拯其溺以救其偏通其蔽以進于
明革其故以即乎新非聖人之風有以激之哉
大哉聖人之道乎遠而不可禦也妙而不可測
也久而不可息也遠不禦故能感也妙不測故
能風也久不息故能孚也夫百世如彼其遠也
風如彼其微也猶能使聞者興起况親炙於當
世者乎頑懦薄鄙猶興而况本非頑懦薄鄙者
乎夷惠之聖且然而况極至者乎於是見聖人
之道教化無窮也夫二子者非一於清與和也

之道教化無窮也夫二子者非一於清與和也
punctuated: 必俟夫聞風興起也邪？惟聖人不常有也，而人不能皆自振拔而有為。由是頑夫遠於廉，懦夫遠於立，薄夫遠於敦，鄙夫遠於寬，拘於偏與蔽而莫反，錮於習而罔覺者衆也。然本心之明未息，同具之理尚存。不有以倡之，孰從而随之？不有以啓之，孰從而明之？幸而百世之上，聖人之風猶傳而弗泯也，則人之仰焉而思，恍焉而喻，翕然而變者，惡能已哉？是故興起于清，則頑可使廉而懦可使立矣；興起于和，則薄可使敦而鄙可使寬矣。拯其溺以救其偏，通其蔽以進于明，革其故以即乎新，非聖人之風有以激之哉？大哉，聖人之道乎！遠而不可禦也，妙而不可測也，久而不可息也。遠不禦，故能感也；妙不測，故能風也；久不息，故能孚也。夫百世如彼其遠也，風如彼其微也，猶能使聞者興起，况親炙於當世者乎？頑懦薄鄙猶興，而况本非頑懦薄鄙者乎？夷惠之聖且然，而况極至者乎？於是見聖人之道教化無窮也。夫二子者，非一於清與和也。
translation_en:
…must they wait to hear of the sages’ exemplary influence before being stirred to action? Yet sages do not always appear, and not everyone can lift himself up and accomplish something. Thus the obstinate remain far from integrity, the weak far from standing firm, the ungenerous far from generosity, and the narrow-minded far from magnanimity. Many are confined by partiality and obscured understanding without turning back, or imprisoned by habit without awakening. Yet the light of their original minds has not gone out, and the principle they share alike still endures. Unless someone leads them, whom will they follow? Unless someone awakens them, through whom will they attain understanding? Fortunately, the exemplary influence of sages a hundred generations past is still transmitted and has not vanished. How, then, could people cease to look up to them and reflect, suddenly comprehend, and readily undergo transformation? Thus, when stirred by purity, the obstinate can be made upright and the weak made resolute; when stirred by harmony, the ungenerous can be made generous and the narrow-minded made magnanimous. To rescue them from what engulfs them and correct their partiality, to clear away their obstructions and advance them toward understanding, to reform their old ways and bring them to renewal—is this not accomplished through the stimulus of the sages’ exemplary influence?

Great indeed is the Way of the sages! Though distant, it cannot be resisted; subtle, it cannot be fathomed; enduring, it cannot be extinguished. Because distance does not impede it, it can move people; because its subtlety cannot be fathomed, it can transform them through example; because its endurance never ceases, it can inspire trust. A hundred generations are so remote, and exemplary influence is so imperceptible, yet it can still stir those who hear of it to action. How much more, then, those who receive a sage’s teaching personally in his own age! Even the obstinate, weak, ungenerous, and narrow-minded are stirred; how much more those who were never such to begin with! Even the sagehood of Boyi and Liuxia Hui can accomplish this; how much more that of one who has reached the utmost perfection! Here we see that the teaching and transforming power of the sages’ Way is inexhaustible. As for these two masters, they were not confined solely to purity and harmony respectively.

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
不念舊惡怨是用希清者之量也直道而事人
不以三公易其介和者之節也使清而無量和
而無節是乃拘方之士迂曲之民非所以語聖
德之至也其何能遺風於百世而使人興起也
哉孟子亟稱二子者何也救時之藥言也夫國
醫之用藥也寒則温之熱則凉之實則瀉之虛
則補之惟其時而已矣戰國之時何時也正道
榛蕪楊墨塞路民方陷溺而不能自振况乎楊
氏為我疑於清墨氏兼愛疑於和聖軌弗昭道
===
真攸蝕安知當世之士不有援夷惠之聖附於
楊墨之說者邪茲固軻之所甚憂也表二子之
聖盖昭道真以翼聖軌也其亦反經之意與雖
然性善則稱堯舜征伐則言湯武王政則師文
王拯亂救世之功則歸禹周公孔子至其自任
則欲距楊墨以繼三聖道統之傳願學之意各
有指叙而夷惠不與焉斯固去取之微權也故
曰稱夷惠者救時之藥言也

表
punctuated:
「不念舊惡，怨是用希」，清者之量也；「直道而事人」，「不以三公易其介」，和者之節也。使清而無量，和而無節，是乃拘方之士、迂曲之民，非所以語聖德之至也，其何能遺風於百世而使人興起也哉？孟子亟稱二子者何也？救時之藥言也。夫國醫之用藥也，寒則温之，熱則凉之，實則瀉之，虛則補之，惟其時而已矣。戰國之時何時也？正道榛蕪，楊墨塞路，民方陷溺而不能自振。况乎楊氏為我疑於清，墨氏兼愛疑於和，聖軌弗昭，道真攸蝕，安知當世之士不有援夷惠之聖附於楊墨之說者邪？茲固軻之所甚憂也。表二子之聖，盖昭道真以翼聖軌也，其亦反經之意與？雖然，性善則稱堯舜，征伐則言湯武，王政則師文王，拯亂救世之功則歸禹、周公、孔子。至其自任，則欲距楊墨以繼三聖。道統之傳、願學之意，各有指叙，而夷惠不與焉。斯固去取之微權也。故曰：稱夷惠者，救時之藥言也。

表
translation_en:
“He did not remember old wrongs, and thus resentment was rare”: this was the magnanimity of the pure sage. “He served others by the straight Way” and “would not exchange his integrity for the rank of one of the Three Dukes”: this was the principled resolve of the harmonious sage. If purity lacked magnanimity and harmony lacked resolve, these would merely be men confined by rigid rules, people of narrow and tortuous understanding; one could not speak of them as possessing the perfection of sagely virtue. How could they leave an enduring influence through a hundred generations and inspire people to rise to goodness?

Why did Mengzi repeatedly praise these two men? His words were medicine to remedy the ills of his age. When a master physician administers medicine, he warms what is cold, cools what is hot, purges excess, and replenishes deficiency. He does only what the circumstances require. What sort of age was the Warring States period? The correct Way was overgrown with weeds, and the teachings of Yang Zhu and Mo Di blocked the road. The people were sinking into error and could not rouse themselves. Moreover, Yang’s doctrine of acting for oneself could be mistaken for purity, and Mo’s doctrine of impartial love could be mistaken for harmony. The sages’ guiding principles were obscured, and the truth of the Way was eroded. How could one know that scholars of that age would not invoke the sageliness of Boyi and Liu Xiahui to lend support to the doctrines of Yang and Mo? This was indeed what deeply troubled Meng Ke. By displaying the sageliness of these two men, he made clear the truth of the Way and upheld the sages’ guiding principles. Was this not also intended to restore the constant norms?

Nevertheless, when discussing the goodness of human nature, he praised Yao and Shun; when discussing punitive campaigns, he spoke of Tang and Wu; and for kingly government, he took King Wen as his model. He attributed the achievements of quelling disorder and saving the world to Yu, the Duke of Zhou, and Kongzi. As for the responsibility he took upon himself, he wished to repel Yang and Mo and thereby carry on the work of these three sages. In the transmission of the succession of the Way and in his declared aspirations to emulate others, each had its particular designation and ordering [?], and Boyi and Liu Xiahui were not included. This was indeed a subtle exercise of judgment in deciding what to reject and what to adopt. Thus I say: his praise of Boyi and Liu Xiahui was medicinal counsel to remedy the ills of his age.

考試官左庶子郭批：典麗敷腴，有唐人矩度，四六之最優者。
貞觀七年正月某日，具官臣某等伏蒙賜宴於玄武門者。伏以：王者治定功成，上下極交歡之泰；聖人父天母地，華夷均一視之仁。解澤旁流，需雲宴樂。肆聞樂而知德，見偃武而修文。宇宙同春，章縫創見。臣等誠歡誠忭，稽首頓首上言：竊惟君臣之分有定，而股肱元首寔一體以相成；内外之限盖嚴，而含齒食毛宜並育而不害。故也天交泰，造化所以
translation_en:
Memorial of thanks by court officials, composed as if on the Tang occasion of a banquet at Xuanwu Gate for officials of rank three and above, regional governors, and chieftains of the Man and Yi peoples, with performances of the dances of the Seven Virtues and the Nine Achievements. 〔Seventh year of Zhenguan〕
He Zishou
Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Instructor: “Pure and antique, classical and disciplined; reading it makes one forget weariness. An excellent example of the memorial form.”
Comment by Examiner Qin, Senior Compiler: “Its ornate parallel prose possesses a dignified bearing.”
Comment by Examiner Guo, Left Secretariat Supervisor: “Classically elegant, expansive and rich, it observes the standards of Tang writers. Among the finest examples of four-and-six prose.”
On a certain day of the first month of the seventh year of Zhenguan, your servants, so-and-so and others, holding their respective offices, have humbly received the favor of a banquet bestowed at Xuanwu Gate. We respectfully consider: when a true king has established order and completed his achievements, those above and below enjoy the fullest harmony of mutual rejoicing; when a sage takes Heaven as father and Earth as mother, Chinese and non-Chinese alike share in his impartial benevolence. The beneficent waters of Deliverance spread everywhere; beneath the clouds of Waiting, we feast and rejoice. Thus, hearing the music, we recognize your virtue; we witness the laying aside of arms and the cultivation of civil accomplishments. The whole universe shares one springtime; we scholars in our ceremonial caps behold what we have never seen before. Truly joyful and delighted, we bow our heads to the ground and submit these words:
We humbly reflect that the respective stations of ruler and minister are fixed, yet arms and legs and head truly form one body, each enabling the others to function. The boundary between those within and those without is indeed strict, yet all who have teeth and eat what grows upon the earth should be nurtured together without harming one another. Thus, earth and Heaven join in harmony [?], whereby the transforming and generative powers …

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
時成必胡越一家王德然後為大粵稽有
道之世聿弘無外之仁岳牧之都俞不廢
三苗之叙羣工之敷命終紀四夷之賓大
國聘小國朝必隆其錫予之典曰來王若
來享咸待以不治之恩秦漢以來處周道
降堂陛峻而聯屬之意微藩籬疎而臣伏
之事寡橫汾歌沛誇得志以狎臣鄰却貢
閉關飾撝謙以謝戎虜是皆心未免於雜
霸故其道終愧于大同兹蓋伏遇
===
〇〇〇〇
健質天成
英姿神授
戎衣一着握旋乾轉坤之功
衮職重明成雷厲風行之化
述作兼乎明聖
仁義法乎陰陽凡有血氣莫不尊親未及百
年已興禮樂邇人安而遠人格車同軌而

===
○○○○
健質天成
英姿神授
戎衣一着握旋乾轉坤之功
衮職重明成雷厲風行之化
述作兼乎明聖
仁義法乎陰陽凡有血氣莫不尊親未及百

punctuated:
時成，必胡越一家，王德然後為大。粵稽有道之世，聿弘無外之仁。岳牧之都俞，不廢三苗之叙；羣工之敷命，終紀四夷之賓。大國聘，小國朝，必隆其錫予之典；曰來王，若來享，咸待以不治之恩。秦漢以來，處周道降，堂陛峻而聯屬之意微，藩籬疎而臣伏之事寡。橫汾歌沛，誇得志以狎臣鄰；却貢閉關，飾撝謙以謝戎虜。是皆心未免於雜霸，故其道終愧于大同。兹蓋伏遇
〇〇〇〇
健質天成，英姿神授。戎衣一着，握旋乾轉坤之功；衮職重明，成雷厲風行之化。述作兼乎明聖，仁義法乎陰陽。凡有血氣，莫不尊親；未及百年，已興禮樂。邇人安而遠人格，車同軌而書同文。
translation_en:
…are accomplished in their proper seasons. Only when the Hu and the Yue form one family does kingly virtue attain greatness. Looking back to ages when the Way prevailed, we find that they extended a benevolence that excluded none. The regional chiefs and governors voiced their assent, yet did not neglect bringing the Sanmiao into order; the proclamation of commands to the assembled officials culminated in the record of the barbarians of the four quarters coming as guests. Great states sent diplomatic missions and small states attended court, and the ceremonies of bestowing gifts upon them were invariably generous. Whether they came to acknowledge royal sovereignty or to present offerings, all received the gracious indulgence of being spared direct governance.

Since the Qin and Han, the Way of Zhou declined [?]. The steps separating sovereign and ministers grew steep, while the spirit of mutual attachment weakened; the fences of the realm grew loose, while acts of submission became rare. Boating across the Fen and singing at Pei, rulers flaunted their fulfilled ambitions and treated their ministers and associates with undue familiarity. Rejecting tribute and closing the passes, they made a show of modest deference to turn away the Rong and other foreign peoples. In all this, their hearts remained tainted by the methods of hegemonic rule; hence their Way ultimately fell short of the Great Unity.

Now we have reverently encountered Your Majesty—[four circle marks in the text: 〇〇〇〇]—whose vigorous nature was formed by Heaven and whose heroic bearing was divinely bestowed. Once clad in martial dress, you achieved the feat of turning Heaven and Earth about; with the renewed brilliance of your imperial office, you brought about transformation as forceful as thunder and swift as wind. In transmitting and creating, you unite sagely illumination and wisdom; in benevolence and righteousness, you take yin and yang as your pattern. Of all beings endowed with blood and breath, none fails to revere and cherish you. Before a hundred years have passed, rites and music have already flourished. Those nearby are at peace, and those far away come in submission; carriages share one wheel gauge, and writing shares one script.

punctuated: 治宜日中，四海洽朝宗之願；樂以天下，九重茂對育之懷。乃因元會之辰，爰舉一朝之享。内三品而外羣牧，聯几席以同登；左九夷而右八蠻，惟酋長而得預。門開玄武，天轉翠華。快五位之龍飛，羅千官於虎拜。遂使雕題畫髻之飾，稽厥角於宸旒；以至就日望雲之流，震山呼於黼座。然尤謂禮以合敬，樂以徵歡。當此地平天成之時，不可無七德九功之舞。昭武烈於破陳乎？託始干戚，紛其載揚；象文治與贊舜為同符，羽籥燁其交映。于聲容之盡美，知創守之兼隆；即終始之一成，表君臣之相悅。嘉魚鳴鹿，方沾湛露之恩；獸舞鳳儀，復覩
translation_en:
…Your rule stands fittingly at the sun’s zenith, fulfilling the desire of all within the four seas to pay court; you share your joy with all under Heaven, and within the ninefold palace your resolve to assist Heaven and Earth in nurturing life flourishes. Thus, on the occasion of the New Year court assembly, a banquet was held for the assembled court. Within the capital, officials of the third rank and above, and outside it, the regional governors, took their places together at adjoining tables and seats. The Nine Yi to the left and the Eight Man to the right were admitted only in the persons of their chieftains. The Xuanwu Gate opened; the kingfisher-feather imperial banners wheeled across the sky. Joy attended the dragon’s flight in the fifth position—the sovereign’s rightful place—and the assembled officials bowed with the martial dignity of tigers. Thus those adorned with tattooed foreheads and painted coiffures [?] bowed their heads before the imperial crown’s pendants, while those who approached the sun and gazed toward the clouds of imperial majesty raised mountain-shaking acclamations before the embroidered throne.
Yet it was especially held that ritual unites all in reverence and music calls forth joy. At this time when the earth is ordered and Heaven’s work accomplished, the dances of the Seven Martial Virtues and the Nine Achievements could not be absent. Was martial glory to be displayed in the dance Breaking the Battle Array? It began with shields and battle-axes, raised aloft in profusion. The representation of civil government accorded with the music praising Shun, feathered dance-plumes and flutes gleaming against one another. In the consummate beauty of sound and movement, one discerned the equal grandeur of founding the dynasty and preserving it; in a complete performance from beginning to end, the mutual delight of ruler and ministers was expressed. Through the songs Fine Fish and Deer Calling, we had just received the grace of Abundant Dew; with beasts dancing and phoenixes appearing in stately array, we beheld once more…

translation_en:
…the music of Heaven’s central court. This is indeed an exceptional favor bestowed by the imperial court, truly a magnificent spectacle in the human world. We, your servants, have been fortunate to draw near Your Majesty’s radiant presence and privileged to attend this grand ceremony. Drinking the special provisions of the imperial kitchen, we feel shame at the admonition in “Cutting Sandalwood,” against enjoying sustenance without earning it; seeing the vile enemy come to court, we are ashamed to have rendered no battlefield service. How could we fail to take seriously the warning against ease and indulgence, thereby repaying the particular favor of Your Majesty’s boundless beneficence? We shall attend to the duties of our stations, serve with reverence, and put remuneration last.

We humbly wish that Your Majesty, occupying the center, will plan for greatness, exercise care at the beginning and consider the end, maintain harmonious order within and awe-inspiring authority abroad, and preserve the foundations of peace, wealth, honor, and glory. May the people become like Huangdi and Shun, and the age be bright and harmonious, with all sharing the blessings of affection for their kin, esteem for the worthy, happiness, and prosperity. Then the spirit of “Wild Ducks” and “Already Drunk” will be seen again today, and the glorious achievement of providing careful plans for posterity will surely endure undiminished for ten thousand years. We, your servants, gaze toward Heaven and look up to Your sacred Majesty, overcome with fervent emotion and reverent awe. We respectfully present this memorial to express our thanks, in order to …

第叁塲。策五道。第一問。陳有年。

…to report to the throne.

Third Session. Five Policy Questions. First Question. Chen Younian.

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: “The way of revering Heaven and diligently caring for the people is fully comprehended in benevolence and sincerity. The grand designs of our Imperial Progenitor and the glorious achievements of His Majesty are not easily extolled by their servants and subjects. Yet this policy essay answers each point thoroughly and in detail, fully revealing their profound significance. It is indeed a masterpiece.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Wei, Instructor: “The sincerity with which our Sagely Progenitor and His Majesty reverently serve Heaven, and their policies of generous solicitude for the people, all originate in the subtle principles of the learning of the mind. This composition expounds these clearly and fully; it should be recorded as a model.”

Comment by Examiner Qin, Senior Compiler: “In revering Heaven and diligently caring for the people, His Majesty accords with the true intentions of the Imperial Progenitor [?]. This composition respectfully recounts and extols these accomplishments. At its conclusion, it further traces their foundation to the learning of reverent unity (jingyi). Its author has evidently benefited from immersion in the sage ruler’s transforming influence and truly deserves to be called an outstanding scholar.”

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官左庶子郭批此作能揄揚我
皇祖
皇上契古帝王心法精蘊誠為有見宜錄以傳
帝王之敬天也以誠而其勤民也以仁夫
惟誠也視於無形聽於無聲所以昭事對
越之忱宥密而匪懈惟仁也容之如天載
之如地所以保綏奠麗之惠廣博而無疆
由是誠積而天心益格仁溥而民心永懷
此體信達順之道中和位育之功
===
聖祖作之於前
皇上纘之於後真足以超近代而匹隆古者也
猗與盛哉愚也嘗誦典謨雅頌之文而知
古帝王之致治矣其道在於敬天而勤民
夫何以曰在敬天也天之高高在上幽遠
茫昧若無與也而聰明明威常監乎下焉
故曰皇天無親克敬惟親聖人虔恭寅畏
不敢自逸者非矯也誠也何以曰在勤民
也民之林林而生蠢樸微眇若可遺也而

translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Guo, Left Vice Mentor: This composition ably extols how our imperial ancestor and His Majesty accord with the profound essentials of the ancient emperors’ and kings’ teachings of the mind. It truly shows insight and should be recorded for transmission.

Emperors and kings revere Heaven through sincerity and diligently care for the people through benevolence. Through sincerity alone, they see what has no form and hear what has no sound; thus their devotion in illustriously serving Heaven and standing before it is profound, quiet, and unremitting. Through benevolence alone, they embrace the people as Heaven does and bear them up as Earth does; thus their beneficence in protecting, pacifying, and securely settling them is broad and boundless. As sincerity accumulates, Heaven’s heart is increasingly moved; as benevolence spreads, the people’s hearts remain ever attached. This is the Way of embodying trustworthiness and attaining accord, and the achievement of centrality and harmony whereby Heaven and Earth take their proper places and all things are nurtured. Our sagely progenitor initiated it, and His Majesty has continued it. Truly, this suffices to surpass recent ages and equal high antiquity. Ah, how magnificent!

I, in my humble understanding, have recited the Canons and Counsels of the Book of Documents and the Odes and Hymns of the Book of Poetry, and have thereby come to understand how the ancient emperors and kings achieved good government. Their Way lay in revering Heaven and diligently caring for the people. Why say that it lay in revering Heaven? Heaven is high, high above, remote, obscure, and indistinct, seemingly uninvolved; yet its hearing and sight, its manifest majesty, constantly watch over the world below. Thus it is said: “August Heaven has no favorites; it favors only those capable of reverence.” That the sage is devout, respectful, vigilant, and fearful, never daring to indulge in ease, is no affectation: it is sincerity. Why say that it lay in diligently caring for the people? The people live in their multitudes, simple, unsophisticated, and insignificant, seemingly such as might be disregarded, yet …

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
休養生息咸賴於上焉故曰民罔常懷懷
于有仁聖人勞來安輯不敢少忽者非過
也仁也今質之詩書有曰欽若昊天也勅
天之命也克謹天戒也小心翼翼昭事上
帝也畏天之威于時保之也帝王之所以
敬天者何如其至也有曰敬授人時也從
欲以治也荒度土功也即康功田功也散
財發粟也帝王之所以勤民者何如其篤
也唐虞致雍熈之盛三代稱有道之長豈
===

宋之仁宗號為法古致治者文帝始具耕
桑之儀定賑窮養老之令下勸農免租之
詔似幾於古矣然沿祀五畤而畧於上帝
非正也獨恭儉愛民有足取焉太宗耕籍
東郊卻罷封禪遣使賑饑除鞭背刑遂有
貞觀之效顧内多慚德漸不克終論者不
能無遺恨焉仁宗祀南郊饗明堂頗合於
典禮賑流民節浮費亦幾於愛民但初年

…their sustenance, recuperation, and increase all depend upon the ruler above. Thus it is said: “The people do not cherish any one ruler constantly; they cherish the one who possesses benevolence.” That the sage comforts and encourages them, settles them in peace, and dares not neglect them in the slightest is no excess: it is benevolence. Now, examining this against the Odes and the Documents, we find these sayings: “Reverently accord with August Heaven”; “Heed Heaven’s mandate”; “Be scrupulously attentive to Heaven’s warnings”; “With careful reverence, illustriously serve the Lord on High”; and “Fear Heaven’s majesty, and thereby preserve what you possess.” How consummate was the reverence for Heaven shown by those emperors and kings! There are also these sayings: “Reverently impart to the people the seasons”; “Govern in accordance with their desires”; “Plan the works upon the land on a grand scale”; “Apply yourself to the work of securing the people’s welfare and to agricultural work”; and “Distribute wealth and issue grain.” How devoted were those emperors and kings in their care for the people! Tang and Yu attained the fullness of harmony and peace, and the Three Dynasties were renowned for their enduring rule in accordance with the Way. Was this not the source of their success?

Among later rulers, Emperor Wen of Han, Taizong of Tang, and Renzong of Song were acclaimed for achieving good government by emulating antiquity. Emperor Wen first established the ceremonies of ploughing and sericulture, instituted ordinances for relieving the poor and supporting the elderly, and issued edicts encouraging agriculture and remitting land taxes. He seemed close to the ancient ideal. Yet he continued sacrifices at the Five Altars while neglecting the Lord on High: this was not correct. It was only his reverence, frugality, and love for the people that merited praise. Taizong ploughed the imperial ritual field in the eastern suburbs, declined and cancelled the Feng and Shan sacrifices, dispatched envoys to relieve famine, and abolished flogging on the back. Thus he achieved the results of the Zhenguan reign. Yet in his private conduct there was much to be ashamed of, and gradually he failed to carry his good beginnings through to the end. Those who assess him cannot but feel lingering regret. Renzong sacrificed in the southern suburbs and made offerings in the Hall of Light, largely in accord with the prescribed rites. He relieved displaced people and curtailed unnecessary expenditure, also approaching the ideal of loving the people. But in the early years…

始終如一其遠於衰弱者幾何哉是三君
者於古帝王之道僅得其粗迹之彷彿耳

translation_en:
…government was not in his own hands, and later troubles multiplied on the western frontier. Had he not remained reverent, frugal, benevolent, and forbearing, consistent from beginning to end, how far would he have stood from decline and weakness? These three rulers attained only a rough semblance of the outward practices of the ancient emperors and kings. Yet this was enough to prolong their dynasties’ allotted span and secure the foundations of their states. How much more could those accomplish who grasped the subtle essence of that Way and put its highest principles into practice?
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao, endowed with divine sagacity, encountered the disorders of the non-Chinese Yuan dynasty, swept away the baleful forces, and established the Chinese realm. His virtue was already sagely, and his governance had already reached perfection. Even so, he remained anxiously diligent, vigilant, and earnest, never allowing himself complacency. When announcing and offering sacrifice at the southern suburban altar, he admonished the officials with the words, “With a single heart, stand before the Lord on High, with sincerity and reverence alone.” Thus the principle linking Heaven and humanity was made clear. Discussing the responses of the various signs described in the “Great Plan” chapter of the Book of Documents, he made “cultivating human affairs below and conforming to Heaven’s Way above” the foundation for reaching Heaven. Thus the subtle workings of sympathetic communication were made manifest. Discussing the practical work of self-cultivation and examination in response to disasters and anomalies, he spoke of “embodying Heaven’s Way and turning disaster into auspiciousness.” Thus he grasped the essentials of self-examination. Was this not the sincerity with which the ancient emperors and kings revered Heaven?
Because the people had lost their livelihoods, he instructed the officials of the Secretariat: “Long afflicted by warfare, they have yet to secure their means of subsistence. Those who stand above others must surely keep this in mind.” This was precisely the concern expressed in “the common people lament.” Because the realm had only just been pacified, he instructed the prefects and magistrates who came to court: “The common people’s wealth and strength are both exhausted; what matters is to nurture them in peace and let them rest…”

When concerned about the calamities of rain or drought, he gives full expression to his sincerity in supplication at the altar of purification. When discerning the first signs of auspicious portents, he devotes himself to the substantive work of cultivating virtue in response to Heaven. This sincerity is precisely the sagely founder’s own reverence for Heaven.

When he inspects the crops in the inner gardens, the Record on “Against Idleness” and the “Airs of Bin” is composed, clarifying the lessons and admonitions concerning diligence and ease. When he feels concern for the farming villages, an edict on agriculture, sericulture, and the prohibition of extravagance is promulgated, making manifest the essential principles of attending to the foundations of livelihood and economizing in expenditure. When he considers the illnesses of the poor, he bestows medicines, bringing those threatened by premature death and pestilence into a realm of benevolence and longevity. When he hears reports of famine and failed harvests, he provides relief in silver and grain, saving the displaced from wasting away in ditches and ravines. This benevolence is precisely the sagely founder’s own solicitude for the people. Compared with the sovereigns of antiquity, does he not possess splendid and brilliant achievements!

I have ventured to reflect upon these matters and respectfully expound them. The odes and rhapsodies embody Tang’s reverent obedience to August Heaven and Zhou’s teaching that illustrious virtue alone is fragrant. The earnest supplications embody Yin’s rectification of its affairs and Zhou’s self-examination in “The Milky Way.” As for the records and edicts, do they not honor the foundations of kingly achievement and attend to what the common people depend upon? That the allotted imperial succession should extend for countless ages, and that longevity and blessings should endure for ten thousand years, assuredly has its basis here.

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
令舉事之典不著聖人者出揆之以理不
泥於迹握之以機不拘於時則推之於懸
象而其數可稽焉考之於躔度而其占可
驗焉審之於代謝而其氣可順焉舉凡因
體以立法修人以合天者盖交相賛而不
悖也尚何差殊之有哉故曰聖人以天地
爲本以陰陽爲端以四時爲柄以日星爲
紀先天而天弗違後天而奉天時其所以
鉤深致遠推步脗合而莫之或忒者誠王
===
道之大務致治之鉅典也粤自黃帝迎日
以推策大舜察璣以齊政神禹錫範以協
疇步其數以授時觀其文以察變法其序
以分職而經星七政之行其精盡於此矣
殆夏后之世羲和沉湎廢時亂日則書載
胤征逮至周室既衰重黎失職告朔之羊
廢而不紹登臺之禮滅而不遵七政乖次
而不識孟陬失紀而莫悟大火猶西流而
怪蟄虫之不藏也職此之故天子不辨時

以推筭大舜察璣以齊政神禹錫範以協
疇步其數以授時觀其文以察變法其序
以分職而經星七政之行其精盡於此矣
殆夏后之世羲和沉湎廢時亂日則書載
徹征逮至周室既衰重黎失職告朔之羊
廢而不紹登臺之禮滅而不遵七政乖次
而不識盈縮失紀而莫悟大火猶西流而
怪螫虫之不蔵也職此之故天子不辨時
punctuated:
令舉事之典不著。聖人者出，揆之以理，不泥於迹；握之以機，不拘於時。則推之於懸象，而其數可稽焉；考之於躔度，而其占可驗焉；審之於代謝，而其氣可順焉。舉凡因體以立法、修人以合天者，盖交相賛而不悖也，尚何差殊之有哉？故曰：「聖人以天地爲本，以陰陽爲端，以四時爲柄，以日星爲紀。」先天而天弗違，後天而奉天時。其所以鉤深致遠、推步脗合而莫之或忒者，誠王道之大務、致治之鉅典也。

粤自黃帝迎日以推策，大舜察璣以齊政，神禹錫範以協疇，步其數以授時，觀其文以察變，法其序以分職，而經星七政之行，其精盡於此矣。殆夏后之世，羲和沉湎，廢時亂日，則《書》載《胤征》。逮至周室既衰，重黎失職，告朔之羊廢而不紹，登臺之禮滅而不遵，七政乖次而不識，孟陬失紀而莫悟，大火猶西流而怪蟄虫之不藏也。職此之故，天子不辨時
translation_en:
…the established procedures for undertaking affairs in accordance with seasonal ordinances are not made manifest. When a sage arises, he assesses these matters by principle, without clinging to outward traces; he grasps their workings, without being bound by fixed times. Thus, by calculation from the celestial phenomena suspended above, their numerical patterns can be ascertained; by examining the degrees of their celestial courses, their prognostications can be verified; and by scrutinizing their successive changes, their vital influences can be followed. All means of establishing methods on the basis of underlying configurations and ordering human affairs to accord with Heaven surely support one another without conflict. What discrepancy could there still be? Hence it is said: “The sage takes Heaven and Earth as his foundation, yin and yang as his starting points, the four seasons as his means of control, and the sun and stars as his regulating framework.” When he acts before Heaven, Heaven does not contravene him; when he acts after Heaven, he follows Heaven’s seasons. His plumbing of the depths and reaching into the distance, and the unfailing agreement of his astronomical calculations with celestial movements, are truly a great concern of the Kingly Way and a grand institution for achieving good government.

From the time when Huangdi observed the approaching sun to calculate the calendar, the great Shun examined the astronomical instrument to bring the Seven Regulators into accord, and the divine Yu bestowed the Great Plan to harmonize its categories, they calculated celestial numbers to announce the seasons, observed celestial patterns to discern changes, and modeled the allocation of offices on their orderly sequence. The subtleties of the movements of the fixed stars and the Seven Regulators—the sun, moon, and five planets—were fully encompassed in these practices. In the age of the Xia rulers, Xi and He sank into drunkenness, neglected the seasons, and threw the reckoning of days into disorder; hence the Book of Documents records the “Punitive Expedition of Yin.” When the house of Zhou had declined, those holding the offices of Chong and Li neglected their duties. The sheep offered for announcing the first day of the month was discontinued and the practice left without succession; the rite of ascending the observation terrace disappeared and was no longer observed. The Seven Regulators departed from their proper stations, yet no one recognized it; the first month of spring lost its proper calendrical place, yet no one understood. The Great Fire star was still moving westward, yet people wondered why hibernating creatures had not withdrawn into hiding. For these reasons, the Son of Heaven failed to distinguish the seasons…

司曆不協日諸侯不受職日御不分朔人
事不恤廢棄農時而周官所謂馮相保章
之職曠莫之舉尚安有極其精以察其變
者哉是達天明數有關於治亂之大如此
若夫天文二十一家之說則漢藝文志所
載也其書自泰壹星子經至圖書秘記為
卷之繁凡四百四十有五其可言者如定
一歲之節也則三百六十五日四分日之

…the calendar officials failed to harmonize the days; the regional lords did not receive their assigned duties; the officials responsible for the sun’s course failed to distinguish the beginnings of months. Human affairs went untended, and the agricultural seasons were neglected. The offices of Astronomer (fengxiang) and Astrologer (baozhang), as described in the Offices of Zhou, went unfulfilled, with no one carrying out their duties. How, then, could anyone attain the utmost precision in order to discern celestial changes? Such is the immense bearing that understanding Heaven and comprehending its numerical patterns have upon order and disorder.
As for the teachings of the twenty-one schools of astronomy, these are recorded in the bibliographical treatise of the History of the Han. Their books, from the Classic of Taiyi and the Stars [?] (Taiyi xingzi jing) to the Secret Records of Diagrams and Writings (Tushu miji), amount to a considerable total of 445 scrolls. Among their teachings that can be described are the following. To establish the measure of a year, they reckon 365 and a quarter days, at which point the sun completes its circuit relative to Heaven; they distinguish the four seasons by the equinoxes, solstices, and the beginnings of spring, summer, autumn, and winter. To establish the measure of a month, they reckon twenty-nine days and a little more than six double-hours, at which point the moon meets the sun; they distinguish long and short months through the last and first days of the lunar month, the quarter moons, and the full moon. To establish the measure of a day, they reckon one circuit of the twenty-eight lunar lodges around the earth; through their disappearance and appearance at dawn and dusk, they verify the hours from zi through hai. As for advances and retardations, the moon’s early and late appearances, its quarters and fullness, and separations and conjunctions, these serve to observe rising and setting and to discern slower and faster motions. Thus some assist the arts and inaugurate undertakings, making Heaven’s light shine with purity [?]; some administer calendrical and celestial observations to prescribe the people’s tasks, establishing methods of intercalation to complete the work of the year; and some draw upon Metal and Fire to explain changes of dynasty, inaugurate institutions, and model calendars, clarifying the seasons, responding to Heaven, and following the course of things. Although their accounts differ from person to person and inevitably have their respective merits and faults, all, in essence, perceive something of the causes of what has already occurred and establish rules and theories by which to test their calculations and predictions. They expound the hidden and subtle, reaching far…

之居故於衆星爲最尊自隋丹元子測驗

窺總括，亦焉得而盡廢之乎？此其大都也。
今以執事之所疑而問者言之：紫微、太微、天市，其於天也爲三垣，而紫微獨爲皇極之居，故於衆星爲最尊。自隋丹元子測驗爲歌，則固以大者占帝矣。獨宋天文志取晉志所引孔子北辰之說，以不動之星主之。彼賈逵、張衡之徒，皆以紐星爲不動者也。至後宋儒測筭，則紐星尚差不動之處一度有餘，且亦隨天而旋，則所謂北辰者，實指不動之處言也。遂以爲當舍其明大而以紐星主之，不幾於崇信之過乎？

translation_en:
…to survey and comprehend them all—how could these methods simply be discarded altogether? Such is the broad outline.
Now, to address the doubts raised in your questions: Ziwei, Taiwei, and Tianshi constitute the Three Enclosures in the heavens. Ziwei alone is the abode of the imperial pole and therefore holds the highest honor among the stars. Since Danyuanzi of the Sui made observations and composed his song, the large star had indeed been taken to signify the emperor. Yet the Treatise on Astronomy in the History of the Song adopted Confucius’s statement about the northern pole, as quoted in the treatise in the History of the Jin, and assigned this role to an unmoving star. Jia Kui, Zhang Heng, and others all regarded the Pivot Star as unmoving. Later, however, measurements and calculations by Song scholars showed that the Pivot Star was more than one degree away from the unmoving point and also revolved with the heavens. Thus, what is called the northern pole actually refers to the unmoving point. To conclude that one should therefore disregard the bright, large star and assign this role to the Pivot Star—is this not verging on excessive credulity?
Among the eastern lodges, the Azure Dragon coils along the left; among the western lodges, the White Tiger stands majestically on the right; among the southern lodges, the Vermilion Bird spreads its wings in front; among the northern lodges, the Numinous Tortoise curls its head behind. Altogether, their constituent groups number three hundred and twenty, comprising two thousand five hundred stars, and the destinies of all things are bound to them. Yet Master Shi says: “In the central palace is the Yellow Emperor; his essence is the Yellow Dragon, constituting Xuanyuan, which lodges and flourishes in Chunhuo. Together with the four directions, it makes five.” On this basis, it is maintained that Quan and all the stars below it should belong to Xuanyuan. Certainly, earth cannot be omitted from the Five Phases; yet it too lodges …

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
躔於四方者也而欲尊軒轅以諸星屬之
不幾於分析之甚乎日行周天其數雖有
定也然日躔於一歲之間行周天度未及
餘分而日已至焉故每歲常有不及之分
然宋大明歷以四十年差一度失之太過
何承天倍其數以百年退一度又反不及
惟唐一行采取劉焯以大衍歷推之乃得
八十三年而差一度故程子有言曰曆象
之法大抵主於日月一事一事既正其餘
===
可推是歲行者自然陽積而盈之常數而
差法者極其變以合天者也月行黃道其
度雖常同日也然四時交會歸於黃道而
轉變焉於是有青赤黑白之異名然陰陽
歷代在冬至夏至則月行青道白道所交
則同而出入之行異曆交在立春立秋則
月循赤道黑道所交則同而出入之行異
去交七日其行九十一度齊於一象之率
而得八行之中八行與中道而九故唐一

punctuated: 躔於四方者也，而欲尊軒轅，以諸星屬之，不幾於分析之甚乎？日行周天，其數雖有定也，然日躔於一歲之間，行周天度未及餘分，而日已至焉，故每歲常有不及之分。然宋大明歷以四十年差一度，失之太過；何承天倍其數，以百年退一度，又反不及。惟唐一行采取劉焯，以大衍歷推之，乃得八十三年而差一度。故程子有言曰：「曆象之法，大抵主於日月一事，一事既正，其餘可推。」是歲行者，自然陽積而盈之常數；而差法者，極其變以合天者也。月行黃道，其度雖常同日也，然四時交會，歸於黃道而轉變焉，於是有青赤黑白之異名。然陰陽歷代，在冬至夏至，則月行青道白道，所交則同，而出入之行異；曆交在立春立秋，則月循赤道黑道，所交則同，而出入之行異。去交七日，其行九十一度，齊於一象之率，而得八行之中。八行與中道而九，故唐一
translation_en:
…also courses through the four quarters. Yet to exalt Xuanyuan and subordinate the other stars to it—is this not to carry division and classification too far? Although the Sun’s circuit of the heavens has a fixed numerical measure, in the course of a year the Sun reaches the relevant point before completing the full circuit together with its fractional remainder. Thus each year there is invariably a fractional shortfall. Yet the Song dynasty’s Daming Calendar reckoned a displacement of one degree every forty years, which was excessive. He Chengtian doubled that number, reckoning a backward shift of one degree every hundred years, but this, conversely, fell short. Only Yixing of the Tang, drawing on Liu Zhuo and calculating with the Dayan Calendar, obtained a displacement of one degree every eighty-three years. Thus Master Cheng said: “The methods of calendrical calculation and celestial observation depend chiefly upon the single matter of the Sun and Moon. Once this matter is correctly established, the rest can be inferred.” Annual motion is therefore the constant numerical measure by which yang naturally accumulates to fullness; the method of calculating displacement fully accounts for its variations so as to accord with Heaven.

Although the Moon’s motion along the ecliptic ordinarily shares the Sun’s course, at its intersections during the four seasons it returns to the ecliptic and changes course. Hence the distinct names of the blue, red, black, and white paths. As the yin and yang circuits alternate [?], when the intersections occur at the winter and summer solstices, the Moon follows the blue and white paths: the points of intersection are the same, but its courses entering and leaving differ. When the intersections occur at the Beginning of Spring and Beginning of Autumn, the Moon follows the red and black paths: the points of intersection are the same, but its courses entering and leaving differ. Seven days from an intersection, it has traveled ninety-one degrees, corresponding to the measure of one quadrant, and reaches the midpoint of one of the eight courses. The eight courses together with the central path make nine. Thus Yi… of the Tang…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
行有言曰迒伏相消朓朒相補則九道之
數可知故黃道者二曜交會不易之定軌
而九道者別其名以識變者也至若七政
同爲陰陽五行之精也而五緯退逆始自
周之末造人紀斁而世道日降是以星紀
適常亦失其初觀乎天文以察時變則星
紀之逆順固班氏所謂可以戄然而懼者
邪五星同爲依天而運也而金水行速獨
不經天夕見西方近南則漸遲而留晨見
===
東方近南則漸速而合盖南方爲天之經
金水當之則留逆而不居固漢天文志所
謂三天兩地者邪要之經星亘常而不遷
七政迭運以成歲自七政之變及薄蝕之
災孔子作春秋但言災而不言應及蔡邕
京房之徒始以事類繫之說者以爲萬一
不應啓不畏之心而况黃道爲七政經行
之地其不能無凌犯者固度數使然去甚
近者不以爲異則德缺而不脩非所以爲

punctuated: 行有言曰：「迒伏相消，朓朒相補，則九道之數可知。」故黃道者，二曜交會不易之定軌；而九道者，別其名以識變者也。至若七政，同爲陰陽五行之精也，而五緯退逆始自周之末造。人紀斁而世道日降，是以星紀適常亦失其初。觀乎天文，以察時變，則星紀之逆順，固班氏所謂可以戄然而懼者邪？五星同爲依天而運也，而金水行速，獨不經天。夕見西方近南，則漸遲而留；晨見東方近南，則漸速而合。盖南方爲天之經，金水當之，則留逆而不居，固《漢天文志》所謂三天兩地者邪？要之，經星亘常而不遷，七政迭運以成歲。自七政之變及薄蝕之災，孔子作《春秋》，但言災而不言應。及蔡邕、京房之徒，始以事類繫之。說者以爲萬一不應，啓不畏之心。而况黃道爲七政經行之地，其不能無凌犯者，固度數使然。去甚近者，不以爲異，則德缺而不脩，非所以爲
translation_en:
…[Yi]xing once said: “When emergence and concealment offset one another [?], and advance and retardation compensate for one another, the numerical principles of the nine paths can be understood.” Thus the Yellow Path—the ecliptic—is the fixed, unchanging track along which the two luminaries meet; the nine paths, however, are distinguished by name to mark their variations. As for the Seven Luminaries, all alike are the essences of yin and yang and the Five Phases, yet the retrograde motions of the five planets began only in the closing age of the Zhou. Human order fell into decay, and the moral condition of the world declined daily; consequently, the regular courses of the stars also lost their original character [?]. By observing celestial patterns, one examines changes in the times. Are not the backward and forward movements of the stars precisely what Master Ban described as grounds for alarm and fear?

The five planets all move in accordance with Heaven, yet Venus and Mercury move swiftly and alone do not traverse the heavens. When visible in the evening in the west, near the south, they gradually slow and become stationary; when visible in the morning in the east, near the south, they gradually accelerate and enter conjunction. For the south is the celestial meridian; when Venus and Mercury reach it, they become stationary and retrograde, without remaining there. Is this indeed what the Treatise on Astronomy in the History of the Han calls “three for Heaven and two for Earth”?

In essence, the fixed stars remain constant and do not shift, while the Seven Luminaries move in succession to complete the year. Concerning anomalies of the Seven Luminaries and calamities involving obscurations and eclipses, Confucius, in composing the Spring and Autumn Annals, recorded only the calamities, without speaking of their corresponding effects in human affairs. Only with men such as Cai Yong and Jing Fang did people begin attaching categories of events to them. Commentators hold that, should a predicted correspondence fail even once, it would encourage a disposition without fear. Moreover, the ecliptic is the region through which the Seven Luminaries travel, and their inevitable encroachments upon one another are inherently determined by their measured courses. If cases in which they approach very closely are not regarded as anomalies, then deficiencies in virtue will go uncorrected; this is no way to…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
事天之道其稍遠者不務察其所以然之
故而誇張之以爲異比其不驗則適以滋
文飾之詞啟怠慢之端如漢儒紛紛卒以
藉口談者其何以稱焉盖天道之高遠而
吾能深揆其理則日至之微不難於前知
天運之流行而吾能窮極其變則精深之
思可參於元化故聖人者順天以求合非
爲合以驗天以籌測爲本以天文爲驗筭
之既精驗之皆合則在天之天審而在人
===
之天定所謂經星與七政者可坐而策而
順時布政遇災修省弗恃其一定之形與
其適然之數者其道亦不外是矣後世占
候紀載析爲二途攝提孟陬昏明錯雜既
未能深知其理如揚雄以盡其幽又未能
深知其數如甘石以盡其著而遂以爲識
數不之講則不幾於曠廢大業無以裨益
至治者乎學士大夫必通三五愚生姑撫
拾往籍以復明問如此執事以爲何如

punctuated: 事天之道。其稍遠者，不務察其所以然之故，而誇張之以爲異，比其不驗，則適以滋文飾之詞，啟怠慢之端。如漢儒紛紛，卒以藉口，談者其何以稱焉？盖天道之高遠，而吾能深揆其理，則日至之微，不難於前知；天運之流行，而吾能窮極其變，則精深之思，可參於元化。故聖人者，順天以求合，非爲合以驗天；以籌測爲本，以天文爲驗。筭之既精，驗之皆合，則在天之天審，而在人之天定。所謂經星與七政者，可坐而策；而順時布政，遇災修省，弗恃其一定之形與其適然之數者，其道亦不外是矣。後世占候紀載，析爲二途，攝提孟陬，昏明錯雜。既未能深知其理，如揚雄以盡其幽，又未能深知其數，如甘石以盡其著，而遂以爲識數不之講，則不幾於曠廢大業，無以裨益至治者乎？學士大夫必通三五，愚生姑撫拾往籍，以復明問如此。執事以爲何如？
translation_en:
…the way of serving Heaven. As for those that pass somewhat farther apart, if one makes no effort to investigate why this happens but exaggerates it as a portent, then, when the prediction fails, this merely breeds excuses and opens the way to negligence. The Han scholars argued endlessly and ultimately furnished grounds for such excuses: how could those discussing them commend this?

Though Heaven’s Way is lofty and remote, if we can thoroughly fathom its principles, even the subtleties of the solstices are not difficult to know beforehand. Though Heaven’s movements flow ceaselessly onward, if we can fully explore their changes, profound thought can participate in the primordial work of transformation. Thus the sage follows Heaven to seek accord with it; he does not contrive an accord in order to test Heaven. He takes calculation and measurement as his foundation and celestial phenomena as verification. Once the calculations are precise and every observation agrees with them, Heaven as it exists above is clearly ascertained, and Heaven as apprehended by human beings is firmly established. The so-called fixed stars and seven luminaries can then be calculated without leaving one’s seat. Issuing governmental measures in accordance with the seasons, cultivating oneself and examining one’s conduct when calamities occur, and refraining from relying solely upon fixed celestial configurations or numerical coincidences—all these likewise follow this same Way.

In later ages, observing portents and keeping records diverged into two pursuits; Sheti and Mengzou, the calendrical designations, and the observations at dusk and dawn became confused. People could neither understand the principles deeply enough to exhaust their hidden subtleties, as Yang Xiong did, nor understand the numerical methods deeply enough to exhaust their observable manifestations, as Gan De and Shi Shen did. Yet they then held that numerical knowledge need not be studied [?]. Would this not come close to neglecting a great undertaking and contributing nothing to consummate government? Scholars and officials must comprehend the Three and Five [?]. This foolish student has provisionally gathered material from earlier writings to answer your discerning question in this fashion. What do you think of it, sir?

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第三問
房有容
同考試官教諭鄭批守令師儒將帥方今急務
子能詳悉古今得失末復以教化為言尤探本之論也錄之
同考試官教諭崔批講求文武真才以副我
皇上作人之效學識宏博佳士也
同考試官教授張批守令之善治學校之真儒將鑑
貢將其源流始末推究詳悉而區畫鑿鑿可行非但學之博洽而已
考試官修撰秦批師牧武衛之才有關於民生之大者
===
能極陳利弊如此豈嘗留心於經世者邪

房有容

人君以仁覆天下，盡官人之道而已；人君以誠經天下，妙作人之術而已。夫天下之廣，不可以獨運者，勢也。於是為之師牧，為之將帥，或撫其内，或營其外，凡以安養天下之民而已。官人之法，不能以無弊者，時也。於是乎作其志氣，核其名實，稽古之道
translation_en:
Third Policy Question
Fang Yourong

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: “The selection of prefects and magistrates, scholarly teachers, and military commanders is an urgent concern today. You explain thoroughly the successes and failures of past and present, and conclude by returning to moral instruction—a discussion that especially probes the root of the matter. Accept this answer.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Cui, Instructor: “You investigate how to find genuine civil and military talent, thereby helping fulfill our Emperor’s efforts to nurture men of ability. Your learning and understanding are broad: you are an excellent scholar.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Professor: “Good administration by prefects and magistrates, true Confucian scholars in the schools, and ‘commanders, a mirror, and the recommendation of commanders’ [?]: you investigate their origins and development thoroughly, and your proposed arrangements are concrete and practicable. This is more than merely extensive learning.”

Comment by Examiner Qin, Senior Compiler: “Talent for teaching and governing the people, and for military protection, has a profound bearing on the people’s livelihood. Since you can set forth the advantages and disadvantages so fully, must you not have devoted attention to statecraft?”

Comment by Examiner Guo, Left Junior Supervisor of Instruction: “In this policy essay on men of ability, your response is clear and fully explores the circumstances in all their particulars. You must possess outstanding talent and discernment.”

For a ruler to shelter all under Heaven with benevolence is simply to fulfill the proper way of appointing men to office; for a ruler to order all under Heaven with sincerity is simply to master the art of nurturing men of ability. The realm is so vast that one cannot administer it alone: this is dictated by circumstances. Thus the ruler appoints teachers and governors, as well as military commanders, some to care for those within and others to conduct affairs beyond, all simply to secure and sustain the people of the realm. That methods of appointing men to office cannot remain free of abuses is a consequence of changing times. Thus he rouses their resolve and spirit, examines whether their actual abilities match their reputations, and investigates the ways of antiquity…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
酌今之宜凡以鼓舞天下之化而已故有
明作之功而更化之機寓焉盡知人之哲
而安民之惠存焉人君所以化成天下者
率是道焉耳苟廢而不修者無以奏功偏
而不舉者不能極治此古今人才之盛衰
化理之興廢每不相及也與執事發策慨
天工之未亮而以官人之法下詢承學愚
竊謂三者之臣固奠麗烝民萬化攸畀焉
者敢不悉言以對夫天生民而立之君欲
===
其祐助以綏四方者也君繼天而立之官
欲其寅亮以成化理者也故曰惟聖時憲
惟臣欽若昔自唐虞命官咨牧百揆時叙
后稷播穀烝民粒矣契敷五教倫品遜矣
大禹徂征有苗格矣用是浹好生之德成
廣運之休降自夏商亦克用乂成周之際
郁乎盛矣甘棠保釐兆民永綏菁莪棫樸
成人有德東山采芑之師皆足以匡皇四
國用是重煕而累洽順治而威嚴夫古昔

國用是重熙而累洽順治而威嚴夫古昔
punctuated:
酌今之宜，凡以鼓舞天下之化而已。故有明作之功，而更化之機寓焉；盡知人之哲，而安民之惠存焉。人君所以化成天下者，率是道焉耳。苟廢而不修者，無以奏功；偏而不舉者，不能極治。此古今人才之盛衰、化理之興廢，每不相及也與？執事發策，慨天工之未亮，而以官人之法下詢承學。愚竊謂三者之臣，固奠麗烝民、萬化攸畀焉者，敢不悉言以對？
夫天生民而立之君，欲其祐助以綏四方者也；君繼天而立之官，欲其寅亮以成化理者也。故曰：「惟聖時憲，惟臣欽若。」昔自唐虞，命官咨牧，百揆時叙；后稷播穀，烝民粒矣；契敷五教，倫品遜矣；大禹徂征，有苗格矣。用是浹好生之德，成廣運之休。降自夏商，亦克用乂。成周之際，郁乎盛矣！甘棠保釐，兆民永綏；菁莪棫樸，成人有德；東山采芑之師，皆足以匡皇四國。用是重煕而累洽，順治而威嚴。夫古昔
translation_en:
…weighing what is appropriate to the present—all to inspire and advance the transformation of the realm. Thus, the achievement of discerning and rousing men contains the means of renewing that transformation; fully exercising the wisdom to judge men brings with it the beneficence of securing the people's peace. This alone is the path by which the ruler transforms and perfects the realm. If it is neglected and left uncultivated, no results can be achieved; if pursued only partially rather than fully, the highest order cannot be attained. Is this not why, in ancient and modern times, the flourishing or decline of talent and the rise or fall of transformative government have so often differed from one age to another? You, honored examiners, have posed this policy question, lamenting that Heaven's work has not been adequately assisted and condescending to ask us students about methods of appointing officials. I humbly consider that ministers of these three kinds are indeed those who settle and bring repose to the multitude, and to whom all transformative endeavors are entrusted. How could I dare not set forth all I have to say in reply?
Heaven brought forth the people and established a ruler over them, intending him to aid its work and pacify the four quarters. The ruler, succeeding to Heaven's work, established officials, intending them to assist him reverently in bringing transformative government to fruition. Thus it is said: “The sage is the model; ministers reverently follow.” Long ago, under Tang and Yu, officials were appointed and regional governors consulted, and the hundred affairs were duly ordered. Hou Ji sowed grain, and the multitude had grain to eat; Xie propagated the five teachings, and the ranks of human relationships became harmonious; the Great Yu went forth on campaign, and the Miao submitted. By these means, the virtue of cherishing life spread everywhere, and the glory of far-reaching rule was achieved. In the succeeding Xia and Shang dynasties, too, good order could be attained. By the time of the Zhou, how splendidly these achievements flourished! The governance celebrated in “The Sweet Pear Tree” (Gan tang) brought enduring peace to the myriad people; “The Luxuriant Mugwort” (Jing e) and “The Oak Trees” (Yu pu) celebrated the nurturing of men to virtuous maturity. The armies of “The Eastern Hills” (Dong shan) and “Gathering Millet” (Cai qi) were all sufficient to rectify and exalt the lands of the four quarters. Thus brilliance accumulated and harmony deepened; government was orderly and possessed imposing dignity. Now, in ancient times…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
盛時所以内外寧謐文武並用者豈止岳
牧時亮之欽周官法制之善哉勞來振作
之機在上而不在下明揚時舉之道以實
而不以文焉耳嗣是而下得人弘化之盛
邈乎不逮間有願治之君命世之士史冊
相輝後先間起有可得而言者焉守令之
最著者在漢則黃覇韓延壽尹翁歸召信
臣見於神爵五鳳之間者是已外此固未
易以悉數然吏治蒸蒸莫有苟且宜其首
===
稱矣乎師儒之最著者在宋則周敦頤張
載程顥程頤朱熹上接道統之傳者是已
外此固未易以槩舉然斯道大明如日中
天宋其極盛矣乎將帥之最著者在漢則
衞青霍去病李廣公孫敖之徒征伐四出
足以雪雲中桑乾之恥在唐則李靖侯君
集柴紹郭孝恪之徒威聲遠振足以報契
丹幽并之讐然龍城狼望王庭徙空而陰
山瀚海版圖内屬雄才大畧孝武太宗不

punctuated:
盛時所以内外寧謐、文武並用者，豈止岳牧時亮之欽、周官法制之善哉？勞來振作之機，在上而不在下；明揚時舉之道，以實而不以文焉耳。嗣是而下，得人弘化之盛，邈乎不逮。間有願治之君、命世之士，史冊相輝，後先間起，有可得而言者焉。

守令之最著者，在漢則黃覇、韓延壽、尹翁歸、召信臣，見於神爵、五鳳之間者是已。外此固未易以悉數，然吏治蒸蒸，莫有苟且，宜其首稱矣乎！

師儒之最著者，在宋則周敦頤、張載、程顥、程頤、朱熹，上接道統之傳者是已。外此固未易以槩舉，然斯道大明，如日中天，宋其極盛矣乎！

將帥之最著者，在漢則衞青、霍去病、李廣、公孫敖之徒，征伐四出，足以雪雲中、桑乾之恥；在唐則李靖、侯君集、柴紹、郭孝恪之徒，威聲遠振，足以報契丹、幽并之讐。然龍城、狼望，王庭徙空，而陰山、瀚海，版圖内屬。雄才大畧，孝武、太宗不
translation_en:
…in those flourishing ages, peace prevailed within and beyond the realm, and civil and military talents were employed together. Could this have resulted merely from the reverent assistance of regional overseers and governors, or from the excellence of the institutions and regulations of the Offices of Zhou? The impetus to encourage, attract, and invigorate men lay with those above, not those below; the way to bring worthy men to notice and appoint them in due season rested on substance, not mere forms. Thereafter, achievements in securing worthy men and extending transforming influence fell far short of that earlier flourishing. Occasionally, rulers intent on good government and men of outstanding gifts appeared, lending luster to one another in the historical records. Arising at intervals in successive generations, they offer examples that can be discussed.

Among the most distinguished prefects and magistrates of the Han were Huang Ba, Han Yanshou, Yin Wenggui, and Shao Xinchen, who appeared during the Shenjue and Wufeng reign periods. Those beyond this group cannot readily be enumerated in full. Yet official administration steadily flourished, and none discharged his duties perfunctorily. Surely it is fitting that the Han should receive foremost praise!

Among the most distinguished Confucian teachers of the Song were Zhou Dunyi, Zhang Zai, Cheng Hao, Cheng Yi, and Zhu Xi, who carried forward the transmission of the succession of the Way from antiquity. Those beyond this group cannot readily be listed even in outline. Yet this Way shone brilliantly, like the sun at midday. Surely it reached its greatest flourishing under the Song!

Among the most distinguished commanders of the Han were Wei Qing, Huo Qubing, Li Guang, Gongsun Ao, and others. They campaigned in every direction, sufficiently avenging the humiliations of Yunzhong and Sanggan. Under the Tang there were Li Jing, Hou Junji, Chai Shao, Guo Xiaoke, and others, whose martial renown resounded afar, sufficiently avenging the wrongs associated with the Qidan and with Youzhou and Bingzhou. At Longcheng and Langwang, the royal courts moved away, leaving those places empty, while Yinshan and Hanhai were incorporated into the imperial domains. In extraordinary talent and grand strategy, neither Emperor Xiaowu nor Emperor Taizong …

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
相上下矣夫雲龍風虎各從其類九重意
向四海改觀彼綜核名實思與二千石共
治者宜其有吏稱民安之功崇儒右文歷
數世而愈隆者宜其有真儒輩出之盛以
至經畧四夷除兇雪耻為志者則李衛諸
臣乘時自奮也固其所哉然陽舒陰慘造
化之全功文經武緯帝王之大業彼治止
雜伯王道未純政終仁弱武功莫競與虛
内事外多欲不終者又何恠乎治之不古
===
若也兹我
皇上以
聖神文武之德撫盈成中興之運允釐百工
咸熙庶績遐視逖聽計安元元教養安全
之司既陶鎔而淬礪之矣然率作興事之
未臻其效誠有如執事所疑者夫雄都巨
邑墨綬銅章膺民社之寄者孰非
帝心簡在固宜畢力一心勉稱
上意也何貪殘玩愒至有民弗堪命者可不求

punctuated:
相上下矣。夫雲龍風虎，各從其類；九重意向，四海改觀。彼綜核名實，思與二千石共治者，宜其有吏稱民安之功；崇儒右文，歷數世而愈隆者，宜其有真儒輩出之盛；以至經畧四夷，除兇雪耻為志者，則李衛諸臣乘時自奮也，固其所哉！然陽舒陰慘，造化之全功；文經武緯，帝王之大業。彼治止雜伯，王道未純；政終仁弱，武功莫競；與虛内事外，多欲不終者，又何恠乎治之不古若也？
兹我皇上以聖神文武之德，撫盈成中興之運，允釐百工，咸熙庶績，遐視逖聽，計安元元。教養安全之司，既陶鎔而淬礪之矣。然率作興事之未臻其效，誠有如執事所疑者。夫雄都巨邑，墨綬銅章，膺民社之寄者，孰非帝心簡在？固宜畢力一心，勉稱上意也。何貪殘玩愒，至有民弗堪命者？可不求
translation_en:
…were on a par. Clouds follow the dragon and winds follow the tiger: each follows its own kind. When the sovereign’s intentions turn in a particular direction, all within the Four Seas takes on a new aspect. Those who scrutinized names against actual performance and sought to govern jointly with officials of two-thousand-bushel rank fittingly achieved capable administration and peace for the people. Those who honored Confucian learning and esteemed literary culture, increasingly exalting them over successive generations, fittingly enjoyed the flourishing emergence of true Confucian scholars. As for those whose ambition was to bring the peoples beyond the borders under control, eliminate violent foes, and avenge humiliation, it was only natural that ministers such as Li Jing and Wei Qing should seize their opportunity and distinguish themselves. Yet the expansive force of yang and the stern force of yin together constitute the full workings of creation; civil government as the warp and military strength as the weft together constitute the great enterprise of emperors and kings. Where government remained mixed with hegemonic methods and the Kingly Way was not pure; where administration proved benevolent but weak [?] and military achievements could not rival those of others; or where rulers depleted their domestic resources to pursue affairs abroad, entertained excessive ambitions, and failed to carry them through—why should it be surprising that their government did not equal that of antiquity?
Now our Emperor, with his sagely and spiritual, civil and martial virtues, presides over an age of flourishing accomplishment and dynastic resurgence. He duly orders the offices, brings every undertaking to fruition, sees and hears afar, and plans for the peace of the common people. He has already molded and tempered the officials charged with instructing, nourishing, protecting, and settling them. Yet their leadership of work and initiation of undertakings have not achieved the intended results: there are indeed grounds for the doubts you have raised. Of those entrusted with the people and their altars of soil and grain in great cities and populous towns, bearing black seal ribbons and bronze seals, who has not been selected in the imperial mind? They should surely devote all their strength with undivided purpose and strive to fulfill the sovereign’s intentions. Why, then, are they greedy and cruel, negligent and idle, to the point that the people cannot endure their commands? Can we fail to seek…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
其故乎盖古之仕者為人今之仕者為已
夫聖賢而下恒待爵賞而後勸苟尊官膴
仕未必特加於循良之吏或濫及夫寵利
之徒則所以導之者非其路矣由是浸漬
成習而勢之所趨極重不反雖有豪傑之
才亦將從風而靡也且遠方黎庶政教未
浹所賴承流宣化惟司牧耳今姑息而官
之者果卜式子卿之徒乎望治之地幾為
酬恩取償之區矧觀察而黜陟之者固未

者之聖書聲望是狥反為語利者之捷徑

七聖考課之績不行而已哉意者重守令
之權使不撓於獲上之圖得行其志可也
申久任之法使不萌夫倖進之念膏澤下
於民可也嚴任子鬻爵之規倣古人教養
覆試之法然後用之可也夫然則黜陟幽
明苟有功於民社者雖刺史而三公可也

punctuated: 其故乎？盖古之仕者為人，今之仕者為已。夫聖賢而下，恒待爵賞而後勸。苟尊官膴仕未必特加於循良之吏，或濫及夫寵利之徒，則所以導之者非其路矣。由是浸漬成習，而勢之所趨，極重不反，雖有豪傑之才，亦將從風而靡也。且遠方黎庶，政教未浹，所賴承流宣化，惟司牧耳。今姑息而官之者，果卜式、子卿之徒乎？望治之地，幾為酬恩取償之區。矧觀察而黜陟之者，固未能盡得其人與法也。資格同滯，祗為凡庸者之聖書；聲望是狥，反為語利者之捷徑。甚有私門納粟，如劉毅之對者，豈惟六代七聖考課之績不行而已哉？意者重守令之權，使不撓於獲上之圖，得行其志，可也；申久任之法，使不萌夫倖進之念，膏澤下於民，可也；嚴任子鬻爵之規，倣古人教養覆試之法，然後用之，可也。夫然則黜陟幽明，苟有功於民社者，雖刺史而三公，可也。
translation_en:
…the reason for this? Those who entered office in antiquity served others; those who enter office today serve themselves. Below the level of sages and worthies, men generally require ranks and rewards before they are spurred to effort. If high office and generous emoluments are not reserved for upright and capable officials, but are sometimes indiscriminately bestowed upon those who pursue favor and profit, then the path along which men are being guided is wrong. Gradually this becomes habitual, and the prevailing tendency grows so powerful that it cannot be reversed. Even men of outstanding ability will bend with the wind.

Moreover, among the common people in distant regions, government and moral instruction have not yet thoroughly penetrated. They depend solely upon their local administrators to transmit the beneficent influence of government and spread its transforming instruction. Are those now indulgently granted office truly men like Bu Shi and Ziqing? Places that look for good government have all but become domains for repaying favors and recouping outlays. Furthermore, neither the personnel charged with inspecting, dismissing, and promoting officials nor their methods are invariably suitable. Qualifications and seniority alike become impediments [?], serving merely as a sacred text for the mediocre; exclusive deference to reputation instead provides a shortcut for those who speak of profit. There are even grain contributions made to private households, as in Liu Yi’s reply. Is this merely a failure to put into effect the achievements in official performance evaluation of the six dynasties and seven sage rulers?

I suggest strengthening the authority of prefects and magistrates, so that their efforts to win favor with superiors do not obstruct them and they can carry out their intentions. Reaffirming the rules for long tenure would also be appropriate, so that they do not conceive hopes of advancement through undeserved favor, and their beneficence reaches the people. It would likewise be appropriate to tighten the regulations governing hereditary privilege and the sale of rank, and to follow the ancients’ methods of education, cultivation, and repeated examination before employing such men. Then, in dismissing the unworthy and promoting the worthy, anyone who has rendered service to the people and their communities could properly be advanced from Regional Inspector to one of the Three Dukes…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
行私以誣上者雖科目而必誅可也如是
而吏治不精者未之有也今窮陬下邑建
學立師青衿髦士孰非
聖心樂育固宜蜚英名流迭興繼出也何靜言
庸違弗可底績焉者可不求其故乎盖古
之學者為已今之學者為人夫豪傑而下
孰非有待而後興苟用汲登庸非明揚夫
成德之士而彙征夫干禄之徒則所以率
之者在彼而不在此矣由是大雅逾邈而
===
輪轅徒飾辭有枝葉雖有上知之資猶將
假此而進也且比閭無教養蒙弗端所賴
觀感振德惟師長耳今姑息而官之者果
陽城安定之徒乎風教之源幾同抱關擊
柝之地矧督率而賓興之者固未能盡得
其人與法也絺章繪句祇為錦繡之階毀
同好異反作道真之妬甚至為世詬訾如
叔文之黨者豈惟皓年沒齒窮經不知其
益而已哉意者重儒臣之選使極天下之

聖心樂育固宜蜚英名流迭興繼出也何靜言

之學者為己今之學者為人夫豪傑而下

之者在彼而不在此矣由是大雅逌邈而

觀感振德惟師長耳今姑息而官之者果

柝之地矧督率而實興之者固未能盡得
其人與法也絺章繪句祗為錦繡之階毀
同好異反作道真之蟊甚至為世詬訾如
叔文之黨者豈惟皓年沒齒窮經不知其
益而已哉意者重儒臣之選使極天下之
punctuated:
行私以誣上者，雖科目而必誅可也。如是而吏治不精者，未之有也。
今窮陬下邑，建學立師，青衿髦士，孰非聖心樂育？固宜蜚英名流，迭興繼出也。何靜言庸違，弗可底績焉者，可不求其故乎？盖古之學者為已，今之學者為人。夫豪傑而下，孰非有待而後興？苟用汲登庸，非明揚夫成德之士，而彙征夫干禄之徒，則所以率之者在彼而不在此矣。由是大雅逾邈，而輪轅徒飾，辭有枝葉；雖有上知之資，猶將假此而進也。且比閭無教，養蒙弗端，所賴觀感振德，惟師長耳。今姑息而官之者，果陽城、安定之徒乎？風教之源，幾同抱關擊柝之地，矧督率而賓興之者，固未能盡得其人與法也。絺章繪句，祇為錦繡之階；毀同好異，反作道真之妬。甚至為世詬訾，如叔文之黨者，豈惟皓年沒齒，窮經不知其益而已哉？意者重儒臣之選，使極天下之
translation_en:
…Those who pursue private interests and deceive their superiors may properly be put to death, even if they entered office through the examinations. With such measures, there has never been a case in which official administration failed to become effective.
Today, schools are established and teachers appointed even in remote corners and humble districts. Among the blue-collared students and outstanding scholars, who is not a beneficiary of the sage sovereign’s delight in nurturing talent? Surely distinguished men of eminent reputation should arise in succession. Why, then, are there those whose words are agreeable but whose conduct is contrary, and who accomplish nothing? Must we not seek the reason? The learners of antiquity studied for their own improvement; learners today study for the approval of others. Below the truly outstanding, who does not require encouragement before rising to the task? If, in employing and promoting men [?], we fail to recognize and advance those of fully developed virtue, instead summoning together those who seek official emoluments, then the incentives we provide lead toward the latter rather than the former. Thus the great standards of refinement recede ever farther, while wheels and shafts receive only superficial ornament and language sprouts decorative branches and leaves. Even those endowed with the highest intelligence will resort to these means of advancement.
Moreover, when neighborhoods provide no instruction and the nurturing of the young lacks a proper foundation, only teachers can inspire emulation and invigorate virtue. Are those now indulgently appointed to these offices truly men like Yang Cheng and Anding [Hu Yuan]? The source of moral instruction has become almost equivalent to a post for gatekeepers and night watchmen. Still less have those charged with supervising students and ceremonially recommending worthy candidates invariably been the right men or followed the right methods. Embroidering compositions and embellishing sentences serves merely as a stairway to splendid advancement; disparaging agreement and delighting in novelty instead breeds hostility toward the truth of the Way. Some even incur the world’s abuse, like the faction of Shuwen [Wang Shuwen]. Is the harm merely that men grow white-haired and spend their entire lives exhaustively studying the classics without knowing their benefit? Perhaps greater weight should be given to selecting scholarly officials, so that those who command the highest esteem throughout the realm …

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
望者分教丕變之焉可也慎選舉之法使
德成而上者再論然後官之可也明師氏
之三物六德保氏之六藝六儀使成材也
易養正於蒙可也夫然則道德齊一有隱
伏巖穴者為卜夢之徵辟以風士習可也
有迪屢未同者移之郊與遠方勿使並進
可也如是而教化不興者未之有也方今
熊羆萬旅虎豹九關仗鉞專閫外之寄鼓
鼙興將帥之思臣守封疆者固宜詰戎兵
===
以經禹迹揚耿光而覲大烈也然夷患孔
棘戎心匪茹曾未聞有勒玄塞之碑而奏
陰山之凱者又豈無其故乎盖安邊境立
功名在於良將不可不擇故必有非常之
人然後建非常之功所謂非常者豈一劔
一夫之勇哉仁明知勇為之幹詩書禮樂
為之府是以謀及根本而動在萬全不待
窮兵黷武而已威振殊域矣今求之於世
胄多豢養紈絝之子起之於帷幄多脂韋

===

陰山之凱者又豈無其故乎盖安邊境立

窮兵黷武而巳威振殊域矣今求之於世

punctuated:
望者分教，丕變之焉可也。慎選舉之法，使德成而上者再論，然後官之可也。明師氏之三物六德、保氏之六藝六儀，使成材也易，養正於蒙可也。夫然，則道德齊一，有隱伏巖穴者，為卜夢之徵辟，以風士習可也；有迪屢未同者，移之郊與遠方，勿使並進可也。如是而教化不興者，未之有也。
方今熊羆萬旅，虎豹九關，仗鉞專閫外之寄，鼓鼙興將帥之思。臣守封疆者，固宜詰戎兵，以經禹迹，揚耿光而覲大烈也。然夷患孔棘，戎心匪茹，曾未聞有勒玄塞之碑而奏陰山之凱者，又豈無其故乎？盖安邊境、立功名，在於良將，不可不擇。故必有非常之人，然後建非常之功。所謂非常者，豈一劔一夫之勇哉？仁明知勇為之幹，詩書禮樂為之府，是以謀及根本，而動在萬全，不待窮兵黷武，而已威振殊域矣。今求之於世胄，多豢養紈絝之子；起之於帷幄，多脂韋
translation_en:
…reputation to take up teaching in different places and bring about a great transformation would be appropriate. It would be appropriate to exercise care in the procedures for selection and recommendation, ensuring that those recommended for their fully developed virtue undergo further assessment before receiving office. Clarifying the three objects of instruction and six virtues taught by the Master, and the six arts and six forms of deportment taught by the Guardian, would make it easy to develop capable men; nurturing rectitude while they are still unformed would be appropriate. With this accomplished, moral conduct would become uniform. If men remained hidden in rocky retreats, it would be appropriate to summon them, as worthy men were once sought through divination and dreams, to influence the habits of scholars. Those who, though repeatedly instructed, still failed to conform could appropriately be moved to the outskirts or distant regions, so that they did not advance alongside the others. There has never been a case in which such measures failed to make moral instruction flourish.
At present, myriad companies are fierce as bears, and tigers and leopards guard the nine gates. Those bearing the battle-axe have sole charge of military affairs beyond the capital; the sound of war drums calls worthy commanders to mind. Your servants who guard the frontiers should certainly put their troops in order, bring good governance to the lands traversed by Yu, spread Your Majesty’s brilliant glory, and display great achievements. Yet the troubles caused by foreign peoples are exceedingly pressing, and their hostile hearts are unyielding. We have not yet heard of anyone erecting a commemorative stele at the northern frontier or reporting victory from Yinshan. Surely this has its causes? Securing the borders and establishing meritorious reputations depend upon good generals, whose selection must therefore receive care. Only when there are extraordinary men can extraordinary achievements follow. Does being extraordinary mean merely the courage of a single man wielding a sword? Benevolence, discernment, wisdom, and courage form such a man’s core; the Odes, the Documents, rites, and music constitute his storehouse. Thus his plans address fundamentals, and his actions ensure complete success. Without exhausting his forces in incessant warfare, his might already resounds through foreign lands. Today, when commanders are sought among hereditary military families, many are pampered sons in silken trousers; when raised from the command tents, many are pliant as grease and soft leather…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
奔走之徒徵之於武舉特弧矢馬足之利
掇拾記誦之能而已固宜不能折衝以禦
侮也矧兵不可遥度將不可中御九天九
淵潜動莫測呼吸闔變機不可移方戰養
力非厚犒無以得死士之心未戰養氣非
專制無以司三軍之命苟將得其人而信
任未專多方掣肘則功敗於垂成威弱於
積忌所謂縶騏足而縛賁手也何暇挫敵
人之鋒而奪其魄哉意者養之豫焉類聚
===
而教以古今勝敗之迹山川險易之宜可
也從而擇之精焉試以邊兵之寄或拔於
行伍之尤者可也又從而任之誠焉小過
不求備長城鎖鑰責以成功軍實賦稅聽
其出入可也夫然有能敵愾獻功者則策
勳鼎彝重錄之以垂勸可也有淫𢙢不恪
者則明見萬里勿使苟免以示威焉可也
如是而武功不競者又豈有是理哉雖然
有本也古之明王莫不以教化為先務是

淵潛動莫測呼吸闔變機不可移方𤅢養

者則明見萬里勿使苟免以示威焉可也

punctuated:
奔走之徒；徵之於武舉，特弧矢馬足之利、掇拾記誦之能而已，固宜不能折衝以禦侮也。矧兵不可遥度，將不可中御，九天九淵，潜動莫測，呼吸闔變，機不可移。方戰養力，非厚犒無以得死士之心；未戰養氣，非專制無以司三軍之命。苟將得其人而信任未專，多方掣肘，則功敗於垂成，威弱於積忌，所謂縶騏足而縛賁手也，何暇挫敵人之鋒而奪其魄哉！

意者，養之豫焉，類聚而教以古今勝敗之迹、山川險易之宜，可也。從而擇之精焉，試以邊兵之寄，或拔於行伍之尤者，可也。又從而任之誠焉，小過不求備，長城鎖鑰責以成功，軍實賦稅聽其出入，可也。夫然，有能敵愾獻功者，則策勳鼎彝，重錄之以垂勸，可也；有淫𢙢不恪者，則明見萬里，勿使苟免以示威焉，可也。如是而武功不競者，又豈有是理哉！雖然，有本也。古之明王莫不以教化為先務，是
translation_en:
…mere errand-runners; if men are recruited through the military examinations, they possess only skill with bows and arrows and in horsemanship, and the ability to piece together memorized passages. It is hardly surprising that they cannot repel attacks and resist aggression. Moreover, military operations cannot be calculated from afar, nor can generals be controlled from within the court. Whether high in the nine heavens or deep in the nine abysses, their concealed movements are unfathomable; within a breath, movements close and change [?], and an opportunity cannot be postponed. During battle, strength must be sustained: without generous rewards, one cannot win the hearts of men ready to die. Before battle, morale must be nurtured: without independent command, one cannot govern the fate of the armies. If the right man has been found as general, but is not fully trusted and is hampered on every side, achievement will fail on the verge of success, and authority will be weakened by accumulated suspicion. This is what is meant by tethering a fine steed’s feet and binding the hands of Meng Ben. How could such a man have any opportunity to blunt the enemy’s assault and shatter its courage?

Perhaps men should be trained beforehand, gathered into groups and taught the lessons of victories and defeats, ancient and modern, and how to make appropriate use of difficult and easy terrain among mountains and rivers. This would be sound. They should then be selected with care and tested by being entrusted with frontier troops; outstanding men might also be promoted from the ranks. This too would be sound. They should then be entrusted with command in earnest: perfection should not be demanded over minor faults; they should be held responsible for successfully serving as the realm’s Great Wall and the locks and keys of its defenses, while being allowed to manage the receipt and expenditure of military supplies and tax revenues. This too would be sound. Then, for those able to confront the enemy’s fury and present achievements, their merits should be inscribed on ritual bronze vessels and prominently recorded to encourage posterity. This would be sound. As for those who are dissolute, fearful [?], and negligent in their duties, scrutiny should reach them even ten thousand li away; they should not be allowed to escape punishment, so that authority may be demonstrated. This too would be sound. With such measures, how could military achievement fail to flourish? Yet there is a foundation to all this. text:
教化也者化民成俗之由而文武之才所
自出也誠使今之教者皆倣胡安定經義
治事之齋使先明乎仁義而後及於錢穀
甲兵之實則化行俗美教化洽矣授之以
政王道著矣戡亂以武大勇敷矣昔周之
制大夫卿士更率以將孔門之學皆能有
勇足民是以吉甫方叔顯允而為憲萬邦
祖述憲章復能為攝相卻齊之舉也苟舍

安之策者則執事三者之問皆畢舉矣豈

If today’s teachers truly all followed Hu Anding’s division of instruction into scriptural interpretation and practical administration, having students first understand benevolence and righteousness and then proceed to the practical affairs of revenue, grain, arms, and troops, its transforming influence would spread, customs would improve, and moral education would permeate society. Entrust those students with government, and the Kingly Way would become manifest; employ them militarily to quell disorder, and their great courage would be displayed. Under the institutions of the Zhou, grand masters and ministers took turns leading armies; those educated in Confucius’s school could both exercise courage and provide for the people. title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
以論古人於千載之前矣必有識之士也取之
考試官修撰秦批折衷古人著作得失悉中
肯綮取之不徒以文也
考試官左庶子郭批評品明確議論正大宜錄
以式
古人之著述將以明道而訓世非以矜勝
而要譽也道足以明而世賴以訓則言斯
傳傳斯永矣道之弗能明而言之不足以
訓君子奚貴焉其迹且至於矜勝而要譽
===
取譏於後之人也有以哉是故學術有淺
深之殊議論有純駁之異世代有汙隆之
遭心迹有公私之判審是四者可以論古
人之著述矣執事發策以古人著述下詢
豈以愚生披誦之餘或亦嚌其糟粕也邪
請舉所聞以對穆叔有言太上立德其次
立功其次立言夫立言雖非功德之比固
亦不朽之盛事也是以古之聖賢恒務焉
故曰由周公而前達而在上其道行由孔

述盖立言之權輿也乎自孔氏以來子思

…from Confucius onward, men were frustrated in their careers and remained in lowly positions, yet established enduring words. Thus, were not the editing and transmitting undertaken by Confucius at the Zhu and Si rivers the beginning of establishing enduring words? Since Confucius, Zisi’s teachings on sincerity and illumination and Meng Ke’s writings on benevolence and righteousness have been so pure as to admit no criticism. The emptiness and unrestrained freedom of Zhuang Zhou and Lie Yukou, the pursuit of achievement and advantage by Guan Zhong and Yan Ying, the doctrines of punishments and administrative performance of Shen Buhai and Han Fei, the vertical and horizontal alliances of Su Qin and Zhang Yi, and the extravagant speculations of Zou Yan and Gongsun Long have done grave harm to our Way. How could they merit inclusion?
Among those who distinguished themselves by founding their own schools and whose writings were praised and transmitted to later generations, should we not count Zuo’s commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals and Xun Qing’s discussions of kingship and hegemony? And Qu Yuan’s Encountering Sorrow and Sima Qian’s Records of the Historian? The Supreme Mystery, Model Sayings, and Explanations of the Mean are the great works of Yang Xiong and Wang Tong; the Chronological History and the Outline and Details are the monumental writings of Sima Guang of Sushui and Zhu Xi of Kaoting. These are all the finest products of the philosophical masters and models for historians. That later readers inevitably differ over their relative merits and shortcomings—is this not because learning varies in depth, and discourse in purity and admixture? Ultimately, the gentleman must examine deeply whether their intentions and deeds were public-spirited or self-serving, and whether their eras flourished or declined.
Zuo himself served as a state historian and personally consulted the records. In composing his commentary, he sometimes placed material before the corresponding passage of the Classic to explain how an affair began; sometimes after it to bring its significance to completion; sometimes followed the Classic to clarify principles; and sometimes interwove its passages to reconcile divergent accounts. text:
亦史家之體也此何足以溷其美邪荀卿
稷下稱秀蘭陵廢處其著書也敷陳往昔
掎絜當世崇王黜伯根極領要信六藝之
羽翼也以性爲惡以禮爲僞未免失之過
激後儒斥之固矣不思宗聖衞道實乃傑
儒之守也此何可以廢其長邪屈原履忠
被讒憂悲愁思乃依風人之義而作離騷
上稱帝嚳下道齊桓中述湯武以刺世事

己詞麗以淫雄固之言豈不易之定論乎
司馬遷世掌天官遭刑發憤乃發金匱石
室之藏而成史記上紀黃帝下逮麟趾貫
穿經傳馳騁古今終始盛衰考之行事劉
向揚雄稱其文直事核爲良史之才深嘉

translation_en:
…is also the historian’s proper practice. How could this suffice to tarnish his excellence? Xun Qing was acclaimed as outstanding at Jixia and lived out of office at Lanling. In his writings he expounded the past, assessed his own age, exalted true kingship and disparaged hegemony, explored fundamentals, and grasped essentials. He was indeed a supporting wing to the Six Classics. In declaring human nature evil and ritual an artificial creation, he admittedly went too far; later Confucians certainly had grounds for criticizing him. Yet they failed to consider that honoring the sages and defending the Way were precisely the commitments of this outstanding scholar. How could these faults justify dismissing his strengths?

Qu Yuan practiced loyalty but suffered slander. In sorrow and troubled reflection, he followed the intent of the poets of the Airs and composed Encountering Sorrow (Li sao). He invoked Emperor Ku in the distant past, spoke of Duke Huan of Qi in more recent times, and recounted Tang and Wu in between, thereby censuring the affairs of his age and illuminating the breadth and loftiness of the Way and its virtue, and the connected principles of order and disorder. Sima Qian considered its meaning to lack the Airs and Odes [?], yet to vie in brilliance with the sun and moon: he was simply expressing profound sympathy for Qu Yuan’s aspirations. “Displaying his talent and exalting himself, his language beautiful but excessive”—were these words of Yang Xiong and Ban Gu really an unalterable verdict?

Sima Qian’s family had held charge of celestial affairs for generations. After suffering punishment, he channeled his indignation into his work, opening the collections preserved in golden coffers and stone chambers to compose the Records of the Historian (Shiji). His account began with the Yellow Emperor and extended down to the qilin’s footprints [?]. It drew together the classics and their commentaries, ranged freely across past and present, and examined beginnings and endings, flourishing and decline, through actual events. Liu Xiang and Yang Xiong praised his straightforward writing and accurate accounts, judging him to possess the abilities of a fine historian: they were simply expressing deep appreciation for his achievement. “His judgments of right and wrong diverge considerably from those of the sages”—was Ban Gu’s statement a balanced assessment that gave due recognition to merit?

Late in life, regretting his literary ornamentation, Yang Xiong devoted his mind to the Great Way. The Supreme Mystery (Taixuan) and Model Sayings (Fayan) embodied the utmost thought of Ziyun [Yang Xiong]. Commentators say that his writing is concise…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
而奥義秘而淵闡王基于絕代振天爵于
群倫雖有小疵其所得者盖多矣後世以
桓譚覆瓿之言遂極其譏貶不幾於和聲
者邪講授河汾留情纂述中說之書仲淹
之緒言也說者謂其微而顯曲而當旁貫
大義宏闡教源其有駁雜門人之附會耳
後世因朱子僭王之喻遂為之責備不近
於借聽者邪司馬光論次歷代君臣事迹
以成編年上關邦國之盛衰下係生民之
===
休戚善可為法惡可為戒允哉治世之鏡
也帝魏寇蜀遺屈皓而取雄或乃其意見
之或偏劑量之未審耳小失何足以掩其
得哉朱元晦倣仲尼春秋體例以修綱目
别統系以明大一統之義表歲年以正首
時之體舉大綱以昭鑒戒具細目以著幾
微亶乎筆削之遺也乃若正例之未周變
例之未明或裁定之未及或𣙜議之未精
耳微瑕何足以盖其全邪竊嘗論之君子
