耳微瑕何足以盖其全邪竊嘗論之君子
punctuated: 而奥，義秘而淵，闡王基于絕代，振天爵于群倫。雖有小疵，其所得者盖多矣。後世以桓譚覆瓿之言，遂極其譏貶，不幾於和聲者邪？講授河汾，留情纂述，《中說》之書，仲淹之緒言也。說者謂其微而顯，曲而當，旁貫大義，宏闡教源。其有駁雜，門人之附會耳。後世因朱子僭王之喻，遂為之責備，不近於借聽者邪？司馬光論次歷代君臣事迹，以成編年，上關邦國之盛衰，下係生民之休戚。善可為法，惡可為戒，允哉治世之鏡也！帝魏寇蜀，遺屈皓而取雄，或乃其意見之或偏、劑量之未審耳。小失何足以掩其得哉？朱元晦倣仲尼《春秋》體例以修《綱目》，别統系以明大一統之義，表歲年以正首時之體，舉大綱以昭鑒戒，具細目以著幾微，亶乎筆削之遺也！乃若正例之未周，變例之未明，或裁定之未及，或𣙜議之未精耳。微瑕何足以盖其全邪？竊嘗論之，君子
translation_en:
…and profound, its meaning recondite and deep, elucidating the foundations of kingly rule in an age when its transmission had been broken, and upholding Heaven-conferred nobility among humankind. Although it has minor flaws, its achievements are surely considerable. When later generations seized upon Huan Tan’s remark about using it to cover a sauce jar and subjected it to the utmost ridicule and disparagement, were they not merely echoing others?

Teaching in the region of the He and Fen rivers and devoting himself to compilation and writing, Zhongyan left his sayings in the book Central Sayings (Zhongshuo). Commentators say that it is subtle yet clear, indirect yet apt, comprehensively embracing the great principles and broadly elucidating the sources of moral instruction. Any inconsistencies and impurities in it are merely interpolations by his disciples. When later generations used Master Zhu’s comparison to the usurpation of royal prerogatives to demand perfection of him, did they not come close to relying on other people’s ears?

Sima Guang discussed and arranged the deeds of rulers and ministers through successive dynasties to produce a chronological history. Above, it concerns the rise and decline of states; below, it bears upon the well-being and suffering of the people. Good deeds can serve as models, and evil deeds as warnings: truly, it is a mirror for governing the world! Treating Wei as the legitimate imperial dynasty and Shu as rebels, omitting Qu Yuan and the Four Hoary Elders [?] while including Yang Xiong—these may simply reflect occasional partiality in his views or insufficient care in weighing his choices. How could minor faults suffice to obscure his achievements?

Zhu Yuanhui followed the organizational principles of Zhongni’s Spring and Autumn Annals in compiling the Outline and Details (Gangmu). He distinguished lines of dynastic succession to clarify the principle of a single legitimate imperial succession; displayed the years to establish the proper form of heading entries by season; set out the main outline to make historical lessons and warnings clear; and supplied detailed entries to reveal the faint beginnings of events. Truly, this carries on the legacy of the sage’s editorial judgments! As for any incompleteness in its regular conventions or lack of clarity in its exceptional conventions, these may simply be matters that his final revision did not reach or that his deliberations did not fully refine. How could slight blemishes suffice to obscure the whole? I have ventured to consider the matter: the gentleman…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之處世心迹根本也學術枝榦也議論華
葉也至於時代之遭其諸土地之肥磽雨
露之養乎丘明去聖未遠言稽典禮義存
法戒後世緣茲事實獲窺筆削之趣舍是
茫無所據矣寔經之亞也屈平憫念宗國
繫心懷王大放厥詞怨而不怒其風雅之
變乎荀卿嫉世濁亂不遂大道乃推儒墨
道德行事志可則矣性本剛决自信大過
取節焉可也馬遷幽憤著書摭輯散佚功
===
誠偉矣但語多微刺不能無少望焉揚雄
最號恬於利祿乃甘臣莽且爲劇秦美新
大節虧矣他美曷贖哉王通希蹤聖軌出
處近正使假以年厥就未可量也温公身
係四海之安危顧置之散地徒蒐輯群編
成茲鉅典而經濟弘畧未究厥施君子不
能無遺憾焉朱子固集諸儒之大成者綱
目則以意授其門人而修晩年詮定未竟
後人以其出於朱也而遂謂大成固不可

punctuated: 之處世，心迹根本也，學術枝榦也，議論華葉也。至於時代之遭，其諸土地之肥磽、雨露之養乎？丘明去聖未遠，言稽典禮，義存法戒，後世緣茲事實，獲窺筆削之趣；舍是，茫無所據矣。寔經之亞也。屈平憫念宗國，繫心懷王，大放厥詞，怨而不怒，其風雅之變乎？荀卿嫉世濁亂，不遂大道，乃推儒墨道德行事，志可則矣。性本剛决，自信大過，取節焉可也。馬遷幽憤著書，摭輯散佚，功誠偉矣。但語多微刺，不能無少望焉。揚雄最號恬於利祿，乃甘臣莽，且爲《劇秦美新》，大節虧矣，他美曷贖哉？王通希蹤聖軌，出處近正，使假以年，厥就未可量也。温公身係四海之安危，顧置之散地，徒蒐輯群編，成茲鉅典，而經濟弘畧未究厥施，君子不能無遺憾焉。朱子固集諸儒之大成者，《綱目》則以意授其門人而修，晩年詮定未竟。後人以其出於朱也，而遂謂大成，固不可
translation_en: …in his conduct in the world, a gentleman’s intentions and actions are the roots; his learning is the trunk and branches; and his arguments are the flowers and leaves. As for the age he encounters, is it not like the fertility or barrenness of the soil and the nourishment of rain and dew? Qiuming lived not long after the Sage. His words accorded with canonical institutions and rites, and their meaning preserved models and admonitions. Through the historical facts he recorded, later generations could glimpse the intent behind the Sage’s editorial choices; without these, they would be wholly without evidence to rely upon. His work truly ranks next to the Classic. Qu Ping grieved for his ancestral state and remained devoted to King Huai. He gave full expression to his words, voicing resentment without anger: was this not a transformed continuation of the Airs and Odes? Xun Qing abhorred the corruption and disorder of his age. Unable to put the Great Way into practice, he expounded the moral teachings and conduct of the Confucians and Mohists. His aspirations deserve emulation. By nature, however, he was firm and decisive, and excessively confident in himself; it is appropriate to adopt selected aspects of his work. Sima Qian wrote out of deeply suppressed indignation, gathering scattered and lost materials. His achievement was indeed great. Yet his words contain many veiled criticisms, and one cannot help wishing for somewhat better from him. Yang Xiong was especially renowned for his indifference to profit and official emoluments, yet he willingly served Wang Mang as a subject and even wrote Criticizing Qin and Praising Xin. His integrity failed in a matter of cardinal importance: how could his other merits redeem this? Wang Tong aspired to follow in the Sage’s footsteps, and his choices about taking office or withdrawing approached what was right. Had he been granted more years, his achievements might have been immeasurable. Duke Wen, Sima Guang, was a man on whom the security or peril of the whole realm depended, yet he was placed in an unimportant post. He could only collect and compile numerous writings to produce this monumental work; his broad plans for ordering the state and aiding the people were never fully put into practice. A gentleman cannot help feeling lasting regret over this. Master Zhu certainly brought the learning of the various Confucian scholars to its fullest synthesis. The Outline and Details, however, was compiled by his disciples under his direction, and his final revision remained unfinished in his later years. For later readers, simply because it originated with Zhu, to pronounce it a consummate achievement is certainly inadmissible…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
因其未詳也而遽指以誚朱亦豈可哉用
是而觀則諸儒心迹之公私學術之淺深
議論之純駁時代之盛衰不待較而著矣
豈非尚論之士所當究心者邪若乃勦前
人之緒言逐世俗之浮論而自陷於刻與
諛焉固非執事之所期亦非愚生之所以
自待也惟進而教之
第五問
李江
===
同考試官教諭胡批援古證今欲有司以實心任事仰稱
皇上宵旰至意盖確論也殆抱忠而思以自效者與
考試官修撰秦批人務實心斯可責以實效識時
務者爲俊傑非子而誰
考試官左庶子郭批賢才任事視誠否如何耳子區
畫主於辨實以一人心卓焉有見錄之
執事發策於訏謨遠猶之餘而猶欲聞補
偏捄弊之術豈以識時務者在俊傑邪顧
愚生何能以知之雖然敢不悉心以對昔

translation_en:
…Yet would it be any more acceptable to seize upon its incompleteness and hastily use it to reproach Zhu Xi? Viewed in this light, the public-mindedness or selfishness of these scholars’ intentions and conduct, the shallowness or depth of their learning, the purity or mixed quality of their arguments, and the flourishing or decline of their times become apparent without any need for comparison. Are these not matters that those who appraise the ancients ought to examine closely? As for plagiarizing the residual sayings of earlier writers and following the superficial opinions of the world, thereby falling into either harsh disparagement or flattery, this is certainly neither what you expect nor what I, your humble student, expect of myself. I ask only that you advance me with your instruction.
Fifth Policy Question
Li Jiang
Comment by Associate Examiner Hu, Instructor: He invokes antiquity to substantiate his arguments concerning the present, wishing the responsible officials to undertake their duties with sincere purpose and thus fulfill His Majesty’s earnest concern, which keeps him occupied from before dawn until late in the evening. This is indeed sound argument. Surely he cherishes loyalty and wishes to prove himself through service!
Comment by Examiner Qin, Senior Compiler: If men cultivate sincere purpose, they can then be held accountable for concrete results. Those who understand the needs of the times are outstanding men. If not you, then who?
Comment by Examiner Guo, Left Secretariat Supervisor: When worthy and talented men undertake duties, everything depends on whether they are sincere. Your proposals chiefly seek to distinguish what is substantive, thereby unifying men’s hearts. You show outstanding insight. Accept this essay.
Amid your grand deliberations and far-reaching plans, you have posed this policy question, still wishing to hear methods for correcting imbalances and remedying abuses. Is this because you hold that outstanding men are those who understand the needs of the times? Yet how could I, your humble student, possess such understanding? Even so, dare I fail to devote my whole mind to answering? In former times…

title: 嘉靖三十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
唐虞三代之時風俗敦龐人心朴畧君端
拱於上而臣効能於下各程其力之可至
各攄其志之欲為厥任專一無分外之慕
禹不耻其不能種稷不耻其不能教契不
羡於明刑皐不覬夫平水土實也厥事直
截無意外之虞尹獨任而不為專說驟相
而不為捷周公不敢庇其兄君奭不必信
其友實也實者何也純然為國之心也是
故無益於國則虛譽不足徇有益於國則
===
嫌疑不足避此所以言之必信為之必成
而共底雍熈泰和之盛也自是而降忠信
之道微譎詡之習勝而淳古之治殆不可
見其能致治小康者惟漢唐宋而已漢不
遠乎古唐不遠乎漢至宋則法制愈密論
議愈詳似非二代可能及也然語國勢則
宋為最弱語人心則宋為多變反有不逮
焉者此其故何也夫法制太繁則多牽制
之患論議各出則多緣飾之非是以漢唐

而共底雍凞泰和之盛也自是而降忠信
之道微譎詡之習勝而淳古之治殆不可
見其能致治小康者惟漢唐宋而已漢不
遠乎古唐不遠乎漢至宋則法制愈密論
議愈詳似非二代可能及也然語國勢則
宋為最弱語人心則宋為多變反有不逮
焉者此其故何也夫法制太繁則多牽制
之患論議各出則多緣飾之非是以漢唐
punctuated:
唐虞三代之時，風俗敦龐，人心朴畧，君端拱於上，而臣効能於下，各程其力之可至，各攄其志之欲為。厥任專一，無分外之慕：禹不耻其不能種，稷不耻其不能教，契不羡於明刑，皐不覬夫平水土，實也。厥事直截，無意外之虞：尹獨任而不為專，說驟相而不為捷，周公不敢庇其兄，君奭不必信其友，實也。實者何也？純然為國之心也。是故無益於國，則虛譽不足徇；有益於國，則嫌疑不足避。此所以言之必信，為之必成，而共底雍熈泰和之盛也。

自是而降，忠信之道微，譎詡之習勝，而淳古之治殆不可見。其能致治小康者，惟漢唐宋而已。漢不遠乎古，唐不遠乎漢，至宋則法制愈密，論議愈詳，似非二代可能及也。然語國勢，則宋為最弱；語人心，則宋為多變，反有不逮焉者。此其故何也？夫法制太繁，則多牽制之患；論議各出，則多緣飾之非。是以漢唐
translation_en:
…in the age of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, customs were generous and substantial, and people’s hearts were simple and unaffected. The ruler sat above with hands folded, while his ministers exercised their abilities below. Each measured what his strength could accomplish, and each gave expression to what he aspired to do. They devoted themselves wholly to their appointed responsibilities, without coveting anything beyond their proper duties. Yu was not ashamed that he could not cultivate grain; Ji was not ashamed that he could not provide moral instruction; Xie did not envy the task of clarifying punishments; and Gao Yao did not covet the work of regulating the waters and the land. This was sincerity. They acted straightforwardly, without apprehension about unforeseen consequences. Yi Yin bore responsibility alone without being deemed domineering; Fu Yue suddenly became chief minister without being deemed to have taken a shortcut to advancement. The Duke of Zhou did not dare shield his elder brother; Lord Shi did not have to trust his friend. This was sincerity. What is sincerity? A heart devoted entirely to the state. Thus, where something brought no benefit to the state, empty praise was not worth pursuing; where something benefited the state, suspicion was not worth avoiding. This is why their words were invariably trustworthy and their undertakings invariably accomplished, and why together they attained the flourishing conditions of concord, prosperity, and perfect peace.

From that time onward, the way of loyalty and trustworthiness declined, habits of deceit and boasting prevailed, and the wholesome government of antiquity could scarcely be seen. Only the Han, Tang, and Song managed to achieve the lesser degree of order known as modest well-being. The Han was not far removed from antiquity, nor the Tang from the Han. By the Song, laws and institutions had become more meticulous and deliberations more detailed, seemingly beyond what either of the two preceding dynasties could match. Yet in the strength of the state, the Song was the weakest; in the hearts of its people, it showed the greatest fickleness. In these respects it fell short instead. Why was this? When laws and institutions become excessively elaborate, they produce many impediments through mutual constraints; when arguments arise from every quarter, they produce many faults of specious embellishment. Yet, after so long a period of peace, people have grown complacent and idle, and the abuses of superficiality at the expense of substance [?] have perhaps proved unavoidable.
